speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the course of the past week either the hon. member who asked this question or myself have been outside the house, and I am glad today to be able to take this occasion to correct a misunderstanding which appears to have arisen regarding the information staffs of the Department of Industry and the Department of Defence Production.
As I have indicated previously on a number of occasions, the Department of Industry looks to the Department of Defence Production for the provision of the majority of its supporting services. This includes the information service which relates to the preparation of pamphlets, the editing of reports and the dissemination of booklets prepared within the Department of Industry. The information division of the Department of Defence Production serves both departments, industry and defence production.
At the present time the information division of the Department of Defence Production, serving both departments, has eight information officers, three technical administrative staff and five clerical and typing employees. Four more information officers have been appointed and will report for duty shortly. There are, however, no plans to augment the present staff further in the next few months. We will only add to staff as need becomes evident and, of course, within the approved establishment.

subtopic: SIGHT REQUIREMENTS FOR PRIVATE PILOT'S LICENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend asked a question with respect to the licensing of private airplane pilots who possess monocular vision. I am advised by my department that the physical standards for civil pilots are set up by the Department of Transport and that these follow closely the international civil aviation organization standards and recommended practices for personnel licensing.
In these standards pilots are required to have vision in both eyes. However, there are some applicants who have vision in only one eye, as a result of which we are asking advice from the defence research board panel on visual problems, which I understand has such an item on the agenda for its meeting in Toronto on November 7. We understand the defence research board is working in close co-operation with the R.C.A.F. institute of aviation medicine.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take up too much time of the committee, but I wish to bring to the attention of the committee a matter to which I referred in debate on May 10, 1961, when the estimates of this department were taken up. My particular reference is to historic sites and to Fort Ellice in my constituency. Some 133 years ago a fort was built on the banks of the Assiniboine just five miles down from the junction with the Qu'Appelle river, and this fort served for 50 years as a stop-off between Winnipeg and Edmonton. Red River carts coming in for furs travelled from Winnipeg to Edmonton. It was a stop-off place; it was on a waterway between Winnipeg and Fort Ellice. It also served as an Indian trading post. Perhaps I may briefly mention that it had a trading post, a carpenter's shop, men's quarters, belfry, cottage, blacksmith's shop, chief factor's house, dairy, storehouses, warehouse and flagstaff. It was fully equipped to serve the area before it was opened to settlers from eastern Canada or Europe.
This site, which I consider to be an historic site, has been considered a number of times by the historic sites and monuments board of Canada. In 1936 the board considered it and for some reason or other decided to do nothing about it. In 1958 Monsignor A. d'Eschambault was instructed by the board "to study the situation especially in connection with the role played by Fort Ellice in supplying pemmican for the fur trade economy". I believe the board received a report in this connection. In 1960 the board considered Fort Ellice among ten other sites, and placed it in ninth position.
This is either an historic site or it is not. Placing Fort Ellice even in ninth place is an admission that it is an historic site, and nothing at all has been done about it in so far as the historic sites and monuments board is concerned.
However, Mr. Chairman, the people of that area have tried to do something to preserve their past. This fort is only a mile or so from the village of St. Lazare, which is settled by good Canadians of French ancestry. In 1930 St. Lazare and the municipality of Ellice erected a cairn just off the traces that are left of the stockade, and have developed a picnic ground thereon. I ask the minister to find another community in Canada that has on its own tried to preserve what we

Supply-Northern Affairs consider to be an historic site, and which the board has admitted to be an historic site by putting it in ninth place.
Just this year Fowillard Brothers, a firm of businessmen, of St. Lazare decided on their own to rebuild this fort at their own expense. I hope the minister is paying attention, Mr. Chairman. The material for the stockade is there. They intend to rebuild the warehouse and convert it into a museum. They have some 60 or 70 museum pieces already gathered in and around St. Lazare to put into this building.
These people are doing this on their own. As a matter of fact the property on which this fort is situated is registered in the name of Fowillard Brothers. However, they would be prepared to turn it over to the nation, and they are doing this rebuilding on their own without having received a broken nickel from this board which decided to place it ninth on the list. Perhaps the board is waiting until all traces of this fort have disappeared, but the local population is not going to let that happen.
I have visited the site. The area where the stockade was is still visible, as is the foundation of the big chimney and the stone foundations of various buildings that were on the site. I refer to the buildings I have already mentioned. There is a badly neglected cemetery there, one portion being where the Indian dead were buried and a portion where the whites were buried.
The minister's department finances the historic sites and monuments board of Canada, and according to vote 15 some $840,000 has been allotted for this purpose. When we come to vote 15 I should like the minister to tell us to which historic sites this money is allotted, and whether we can expect some consideration in this regard if for no other reason than the fact that the local people and businessmen are anxious to preserve this site for posterity. This site in west central Manitoba is just as important, I feel, as any other historic site in Canada.
With these few remarks I would close by saying I hope the minister will give this matter some consideration, if not in the 1964-65 estimates then at some future time. I have old pictures of the fort which I could show the minister. I could show him the remains of what is left. If the minister were to see those sunken graves he would find just pieces of boards marking the spots. He would not even be able to read the names of the dead buried there. Instead of continuing to neglect and ignore our past and to spend

money on other parts of Canada, I contend that Fort Ellice, which played such an important part in the fur trade of central Manitoba, deserves careful consideration by the minister.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, very briefly I should like to draw to the attention of the minister some of the representations that have been made over the years in reference to the attitude of the province of Alberta toward some of the national park areas in that province. First, several months ago the minister answered a question I asked on orders of the day and said he was going to bring forward a new statement of policy respecting the development particularly of tourist accommodation within the national parks. If I have missed having this policy drawn to my attention I am sorry, but so far I have not heard of it, I think there is some confusion, particularly in Banff national park and Jasper national park, regarding what will be allowed and what will not be allowed, and how much discretion certain officers of the department have in making decisions as to what is in fact going to be acceptable and what is not acceptable in this field of tourist accommodation development. I hope that policy will be announced fairly soon in order to clear the air in respect of this situation.
The other subject I should like to discuss, Mr. Chairman, is the application the province of Alberta has made to the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources

Supply-Northern Affairs respecting Wood Buffalo park in northern Alberta. That park may not be well known, but the provincial legislature passed a resolution, I think unanimously, during its last session requesting the federal government to turn back this land area to provincial jurisdiction.
There are many good reasons for this, probably the most important of which is that the province of Alberta wants to proceed with some development of the natural resources existing within this very large park area. We must also take into consideration the fact that this area is at the extreme northern edge of Alberta, with a part of it extending into the Northwest Territories. It lies in an area that will never, or at least in the foreseeable future, attract large numbers of tourists because at the present time there is no road into this park of the kind tourists will travel. It lies in an area of Canada where the summer season is short. Circumstances are such that I feel safe in saying that for a long time this area will not be suitable for any kind of development which might attract great numbers of tourists.
I should like to point out that there are some very important and valuable deposits of minerals in this area that could be developed very profitably for the province of Alberta. I might say I appreciate the attitude of the department of northern affairs in its belief that the people of Canada want more rather than fewer national parks, and I agree with that feeling. It is so obvious that more and more people are travelling around the country making good use of national park facilities, particularly for camping and holidaying, that it hardly needs to be mentioned; but I do think that in pursuing this policy which, as I have said, is certainly desirable as far as I am concerned, the department ought to be directing its efforts toward developing more national parks in areas which lend themselves to the prospect of attracting tourists.
At the present time any potential development reasonably close to the trans-Canada highway ought to be given prior consideration, and I suggest to the minister that his department give some consideration to taking over what is known as the dinosaur park in southern Alberta. While I am not authorized to speak on behalf of the province or the government of Alberta in suggesting that the province might be willing to transfer this park area to the national parks board, I think perhaps the province of Alberta would be will-

ing to consider exchanging this area for the Wood Buffalo park in northern Alberta.
There are some unique features about this dinosaur park area which would make it far more suitable as a national park than as a provincial park. It is the only area that has been set aside anywhere in Canada with this kind of historical significance so far as fossils are concerned, and it has attracted the international attention of those people who are interested in the vertebrae remains of dinosaurs several million years old. There certainly is a great potential tourist attraction in this area, and it seems desirable that it be administered and developed by the national parks board. Perhaps I should also mention that this area is located only about 20 miles from the trans-Canada highway, so there is certainly no difficulty in respect of building access roads for the massive flow of tourists travelling across this country every summer.
Mr. Chairman, that is all I want to say at this time in an attempt to make known to the minister and Canadians generally that the province of Alberta does take the attitude that Wood Buffalo park should be turned back to the province, because it will not be developed for a number of years, and that there are other places in Alberta that the minister ought to consider in so far as developing additional park lands which Canadians generally seem to want.

maintopic: DISPOSITION OF OFFICE FURNITURE OF FIRST WOMAN MEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to know that other members of this house are interested in Wood Buffalo park. The greater portion of this enormous land area, approximately 14,500 square miles, is situated in my own constituency of Athabasca. There has not been much publicity given to this park over the years, I suppose for the perfectly good reason that it is not and never will be a playground in the sense that Banff and Jasper parks are. However, this park is the home of a very large herd of plains buffalo which were put up there some years ago as a result of the farsightedness of some members of the federal government. These buffalo have flourished in this area, and it is a pity that they are so far off the beaten track they are practically unseen.
At this point I should like to direct the minister's attention to the fact that Elk Island park, just east of Edmonton, is also the home of a herd of buffalo, but does not receive the publicity it deserves. I suggest that more money be spent in advertising our buffalo herds, especially in Elk Island park. This area is in the constituency of the hon.

member for Edmonton East, and he asked me to bring this matter to the attention of the minister in order to speed up the passage of his estimates.
As early as 1958 I took it upon myself to look into the question of returning Wood Buffalo park to the province of Alberta. I am delighted to hear, though in a roundabout way from the hon. member for Medicine Hat, that the province of Alberta are taking a new look at their attitude with regard to cooperation in this matter, because in all the overtures I made in contacts with officials of the province on several occasions their attitude has always been all or nothing at all. They want the whole of Wood Buffalo park that lies within the province of Alberta turned back to the province without any consideration for the interests of the federal government in preserving Wood Buffalo park as a national playground and as a home for wildlife.
As hon. members probably know, the only flock of whooping cranes in the world nests every summer in Wood Buffalo park. Those who like to use wildlife as a complete argument in favour of the federal government retaining the whole of Wood Buffalo park will say that 14,500 square miles are needed for some 30 whooping cranes to nest. This, of course, is patently ridiculous. We do not even need that much land to pasture the two magnificent herds of buffalo. At the same time I think some of this area should be retained particularly for the wild woods buffalo, but it would be quite possible to turn back the major portion of Wood Buffalo park to the province.
There are vast mineral resources in this area. At the present time no commercialization whatsoever is allowed under the National Parks Act. I am inclined to agree with this as a general principle for our national parks; but if the size of Wood Buffalo park were decreased, which I think is sensible, we would not have to change the National Parks Act. It would then be possible to make an assessment of the mineral and other resources, once a large portion of the area was turned back to the province.
However, I want to say again that before the federal government can act in this matter I think it must have a very firm commitment from the province indicating that the provincial officials are at least willing to meet the federal government half way, so that a long view can be taken of the whole national parks problem for the purpose of arriving at some sensible adjustment. This
Supply-Northern Affairs can only be done, of course, by open and friendly discussion. The closed door attitude which I encountered in this regard over a period of five years achieved absolutely nothing. The former administration finally did get the door open by offering the provincial government a sizeable portion of Wood Buffalo park as a basis for entering into further discussions. However, the election unfortunately interfered with this matter, and I am not sure what the present situation is with regard to taking a new look at our national parks.
I think a great deal more can be done with respect to setting up national parks farther south. In my view the province should cooperate in some kind of land trade. It need not necessarily be acre for acre; in fact a much smaller area might be provided as a new home for the buffalo, perhaps in the Cypress hills or at Wainwright or at Red Deer. Instead of going up a blind alley by talking about whooping cranes, this might be a very fair exchange from the recreational point of view for people who would want to go to such a place for their summer holidays.
I think I would be remiss if I did not pay tribute to Mr. Olsen, the superintendent of Wood Buffalo park, for his magnificent work in caring for both the plains buffalo and the wild woods buffalo which inhabit that region. In the last few years there has been some difficulty because of the ravages of anthrax, which could presumably destroy the whole of the buffalo herd if it were not kept under control. Mr. Olsen and his staff, with the co-operation of the health of animals branch, have been able to keep the disease under control. At the present time they are faced with the rather large and difficult task of inoculating these wild animals. I am quite sure that any expense to which we may be put to preserve these last two significant herds of buffalo will be well worth while, inasmuch as people for generations to come will be able to enjoy seeing these herds.
With regard to the question of accessibility to parks, I should like to urge the minister to use his influence with the other members of the government to make sure that when trans-Canada highway No. 2 is built, as it will be, it will go far enough north to link our magnificent northern parks all across Canada. I suggest that this might be pressed now as one of our national centennial projects. I should like to see trans-Canada highway No. 2 or confederation highway, as I prefer to call it, well on its way, if not completed, by 1967.

Supply-Northern Affairs
I suggest it should link Riding Mountain national park in Manitoba, Prince Albert national park in Saskatchewan and a new park in the Cold Lake area where there is a magnificent lake which is the equal of any other in Canada. I suggest that the highway should then bypass Edmonton to the north, proceed to Jasper park and perhaps fork somewhere in the Whitecourt area with one fork leading to the Alaska highway.
One difficulty that is encountered in setting up national parks in Canada is the temperature of the water in the lakes. With natural gas so readily available in northern Alberta it seems to me it would be a very easy thing to develop large outdoor swimming pools, heat them by natural gas jets and perhaps raise the temperature of the water by 20 degrees. The people who live on the prairies and visitors would then be able to take advantage of these beautiful northern parks for purposes of family swimming at temperatures which are not too cold.
I do not wish to delay the passage of the minister's estimates any longer. I hope he and his department can get together with the provincial authorities of Alberta and take a new look at the readjustment of the size of the parks and the permitting of commercial development. I think also some attention should be given to the creation of new parks farther south in order that we may have a complete chain of national parks serving our people.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say just a few words, not about Wood Buffalo park but with regard to one of the most popular parks in the country, Prince Edward Island national park, about which I have not noted a great deal in earlier statements emanating from the minister. I have been most impressed with the growth of this park and its use during the tenure of office of the minister's three predecessors. Tourism is the most rapidly expanding and most expandable industry in the province of Prince Edward Island, and the federal government is able to contribute mightily through its parks policy.
There are developments of late which have caused me some concern. The Prince Edward Island park is largely a beach park and is recreational because of the bathing facilities it provides and its very fine golf course. It used to have a program which drew appreciative comment from hundreds of thousands of visitors, and I have been alarmed to discover that this program has been abandoned under the present government. It was a re-

creational program, and for many years we had a fine recreational director there.
I have now found that the recreational hall is locked up, and on August 7 I wrote a letter to the minister to which I received no reply. This discourtesy to myself I do not mind, but I must protest on behalf of the people concerned. It is extremely important that the recreation program be not abandoned, but that it be developed. More and more tourists are coming to P.E.I. every year. Local tourist operators are providing more facilities, and there is never any trouble about accommodating visitors. But it behooves the park authorities to provide the best possible recreational program.
I would hope that some imaginative leadership might produce a little more development in the Rustico section of the park. It is an historic village, very old, and one of the unique fishing centres in the maritime provinces. I am also interested in what is happening in the Fort Amherst historic park, which was set up just a few years ago. Fort Amherst reflects not only the English regime but also the French regime, and I find it difficult to see significant or tangible marks of development in recent months. I would hope no opportunity will be missed to develop this park.
Another problem which I have discussed with the minister's predecessors is the enlargement of the present park by giving it greater width or breadth, whichever word is preferable. It is a long strip taking in a great deal of beach, but for many purposes greater depth is required. I believe the P.E.I. government was prepared to turn over land to the dominion government and the department in order to increase the width of the park and provide for greater development, but it is my understanding that this has not been accepted and I would like to know why.
I am also extremely anxious to know something about the second national park promised by the government some months ago, and I would like to know particularly where it is going to be established. Because I want to see the present session end some day before we begin another one, I shall terminate my remarks but certainly not my interest in this subject.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to enter a plea with the minister of northern affairs on behalf of the Minister of Public Works, and in the interests of cabinet solidarity I at once declare that my plea is

entirely gratuitous and not based on any behind scenes arrangement with the minister. My plea is that the minister do something to rescue the Minister of Public Works from the dilemma in which the national parks administration has placed him in respect to the operations of the trans-Canada highway.
This highway runs through several major national parks in the west, and under existing arrangements the national parks administration levies a toll on vehicles entering national parks. This has forced the Minister of Public Works to depart from the concept of a national toll-free highway from coast to coast.
I myself have travelled this highway from Alberta across into B.C., and on the basis of an informal calculation I believe it is the most expensive piece of toll highway in the world, particularly that section in the eastern part of B.C. and the area adjacent to Banff national park. Toll costs amount to roughly $1 per hour of driving time. I have travelled on turnpike roads in the United States, and I know it is possible to travel on them for a whole day at modern highway speeds for less money than that.
I made reference to this matter when the estimates of the Department of Public Works were discussed last year, but inasmuch as the basic decision apparently lies within the jurisdiction of the minister of northern affairs I suggest to him that it is a matter which requires rectification in the interests of the comfort of his colleague, if for no other reason. As a matter of fact I made reference to this problem when speaking to the courteous young woman on duty at the park gates. 1 asked her why we had to pay a toll on the trans-Canada highway. She replied in a most adept manner and I pressed with a second question, whereupon she said "Why don't you take it up with the Prime Minister?" I was sorely tempted to identify myself as a member of parliament but I decided not to, and merely said that perhaps I would do just that.
This may not appear to be a weighty or serious matter. The levy is $2 per year, which entitles one to travel through any of the national parks in the country. Nevertheless it is a matter which should receive immediate and serious attention in the interests of those of us who use the trans-Canada highway for the purpose of travelling across Canada and not for the purpose of visiting national parks.
The minister knows I come from a part of B.C. that has scenic aspects exceeding anything to be found in Banff or any of the other parks in that region. If we in the coastal areas
Supply-Northern Affairs of B.C. want to enjoy scenery we have no reason to travel to Banff.

Later, as a result of complaints from tourists, they were reduced to the amount originally charged.
Many people have applied for posts as park wardens. My main point, though, is that undergraduates who wish to obtain work during their vacations should be given a chance to do so. I am told that at lac la Ronge itself everything possible is being done

Supply-Northern Affairs to attract more tourists from the United States. This is obviously needed, because these people come thousands of miles and sometimes they find it difficult to obtain lodgings which offer them all the facilities they need to enjoy their holidays.

maintopic: DISPOSITION OF OFFICE FURNITURE OF FIRST WOMAN MEMBER
speechtext:
May I take the opportunity to make a few brief comments and ask a few questions of the minister at this time. My remarks all concern Elk Island national park, which lies wholly within my constituency of Vegreville. I suppose I should thank my hon. friend from Athabasca for putting in a plug for this area, one which I had intended to make. He has helped me that much. I do agree that a park such as Elk Island should receive more publicity, as he suggested. May I suggest to the minister that if I am not in my place when he rises to reply to this discussion he should answer my questions and put the answers on the record in full, because as the result of another engagement I shall probably be out of the house when he replies to the points raised in the debate.
The heading of this item, item 15, is "national parks, historic sites and monuments-administration, operation and maintenance of parks". This is the only place where Elk Island national park is mentioned. The estimates contain an item of estimated expenditure amounting to $326,200 to cover all those things I have mentioned and I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that considering all the expenditures which are needed in the parks this amount will have to be spread out pretty thinly. It would look as though Elk Island national park is again becoming the Cinderella park of Canada as it was in 1958, when I came here. After a great deal of hard work-and I certainly bothered all the ministers-this Cinderella park of Canada reached a stage a year ago where that title was no longer applicable. I should like the minister to give us a breakdown, an itemized statement showing what expenditures within that park are included in this sum of $326,200. As I have just said, it will have to be spread pretty thinly; there will not be very many extras this year.
Elk Island national park has been through several phases. It began as a park set aside solely for buffalo. As time went on it became a recreation centre, and because of the extent of wildlife there-buffalo, elk, moose and deer-and also because of the severe winters

occurring from time to time, it became necessary to develop a farming phase so as to provide fodder to keep these animals alive throughout the winter. At one time the herd of buffalo in the park numbered between 1,200 and 1,500. I have no official information, but I have been told that excluding this year's calves the herd numbers fewer than 500 animals at the present time. I do not know how correct my information is, but assuming it is correct I think this is a very small number of buffalo to have in a park the size of Elk Island. The feed situation is always very good there, and I think that park should be able to pasture somewhere between 500 and 1,000 head all the time. I would like the minister to take note of this point, because I have been asked many times how many animals the government intends to keep there.
For quite some years there has been a project afoot in regard to building a museum in Elk Island park. This is something that I think should be continued. I worked very hard on this during the years when the party to which I belong formed the government, and I seemed to be getting somewhere. I just do not know where that item has been relegated to at the moment; sometimes it is rather difficult to find out.
However, Mr. Chairman, there is a small museum there. It is contained in a house of the original type that was built by the people from central Europe when they came to this country. It is very well preserved and well looked after, but it is very small and can house very few of the items that a museum should be able to house. In my opinion this project should be continued and carried to completion, because this area is very productive of museum pieces and there should be somewhere in which they could be housed. There would not be any trouble in getting somebody to look after a museum of that type.
There is also very great need for a large swimming pool close to the lake at Sandy beach. I know that a swimming pool is quite an extensive project, but we must have one because at times the water in the lake is not too good for swimming; there is a great deal of algae, leeches and things like that in the water, and it is just not satisfactory. Provision should be made for a large swimming pool there because most of the water that is available at the present time is not very satisfactory. Water could be provided through the purification system that was installed there in the last few years.

I have also been asked about a second golf course on the park. There is one nine hole course that I believe is very popular; it is supposed to be a very good course. I would not have the slightest idea what makes a good golf course, but many people who play there tell me it is very difficult to get a game on a holiday, Saturday or Sunday because the crowd which lines up to play is so large and is more than one nine hole course can handle. It has been suggested that another golf course of similar size be provide in order to give these facilities to a great many more people. I realize very well that extra things like that will certainly take away from the amount of land available on which to raise buffalo. However, Mr. Chairman, another nine hole golf course would not take up that much room and would not make very much difference. Again I would ask the minister to answer the questions I have raised when he deals with points which hon. members have put forward. I will not be in my seat when the minister replies, but I hope he will deal with these matters at that time.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to speak at length, but I wish to raise a few questions with respect to the administration of Mount Revelstoke park, at the request of a number of residents of Revelstoke including some well known members of the minister's own party. I raised these questions when the former minister was in office. I did get some information, but apparently a number of people consider there is justification for criticism of the administration of this park.
I might say that I do not know the superintendent and have never met him, but I have known the park area very well ever since I was a young man. The previous inquiries were directed to me by the residents of whom I spoke, and I put questions on the order paper. The residents were talking about the waste of public funds and so on, and I believe their contention was proven when as a result of questions that I asked I discovered that the superintendent's house cost $48,000. It has cost more since; repairs and alterations have been carried out on the house since that time. I would like the minister to inform the committee how many park superintendents' houses in Canada have cost $48,000 plus, and whether this is government policy in this respect; because it has been the cause of considerable criticism and I think justifiably so.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I want to know whether it is the custom in the parks for the employees to cut the wood for the park super-
Supply-Northern Affairs intendent and put it in the woodshed. This was brought to my attention, and I asked questions about it. It was discovered that the wood was cut for the superintendent at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada. The feeling apparently was that this poor park superintendent could not afford to buy his own fuel or anything like that, poor chap; so they cut the wood and put it in the woodshed. On one occasion his wife did not like fir and made them take it all out and put birch in the shed. I would ask the minister, is it customary for the taxpayers of Canada to supply the fuel for a park superintendent who lives within a quarter of a mile of a city?
I know a good many employees in this park, and I have been informed that they were set to work helping a contractor build houses while their salary was being paid by the government of Canada. I want to ask whether it is the policy of the park, and I have been informed that they at the expense of the government of Canada with respect to the building of houses and other works in parks. I also want to know how much free labour the government of Canada is supposed to provide with respect to looking after the gardens and lawns of the officials of our parks. If they do not get salaries sufficient to pay for such things like any ordinary citizen, then it may be justified. I also want to ask about salaries. I want to know what is the salary of the superintendent, what are his academic qualifications for the post, and what previous posts he has held. Also, what was his experience prior to being appointed superintendent of the park? I just ask these questions of behalf of these ladies and gentlemen so they can be published in the Revelstoke Review with the minister's reply.
I now come to the administration of the park. In recent years some quite expensive log cabins have been built on top of mount Revelstoke, and I have been informed by someone who worked on them that they cost about $15,000 each. I am also informed that it is now the intention of the administration to tear down these log cabins, which have been very well built. I should like the minister to tell us what is the policy of the administration of the park with respect to these log cabins on top of mount Revelstoke, and to tell us, if they are to be torn down,

Supply-Northern Affairs why they are being torn down and what was their purpose in the first place, this money having been spent on them. I should also like to know what was their actual cost, because I was informed that they cost about $15,000 each.
A new road is being built to the top of mount Revelstoke which I understand is being done by contract. I should like the minister to inform the committee who are the contractors and what is the total amount of the contract. I know a little about road construction, having been concerned in the building of a good many miles of highway a few years ago. Also what is the total yardage of earth, rock and shale, and so on, which is to be moved? I would also like the minister to inform the committee whether under present circumstances any of the employees who work in mount Revelstoke park render any assistance at any time to the contractors, their services being paid for by the government of Canada.
1 expect the minister will not be able to completely answer these questions today, but I did promise to ask them. The point has now been reached where some people are watching the administration of the park almost daily with a microscopic eye, as are some of the well known members of the minister's party. However, I always bring up complaints whether they come from Liberals or Conservatives. While these particular complaints did not emanate from my own party, I did tell these ladies and gentlemen concerned that I would raise them at the first opportunity on the minister's estimates, and I shall look forward to some comprehensive replies. I am confident that it is not his idea that we should be so lavish in our expenditures on homes for superintendents, engineers and other officials of our parks. We want adequate accommodation, but we do not want luxury.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to refer to an application which has been before the national historic sites committee for a number of years concerning Fort Walsh in the southwestern part of Saskatchewan. I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Marquette say a few moments ago that there is a priority list which this committee uses in designating these historic sites. Although Fort Walsh is not recognized by the committee as an historic site, I think all hon. members of the committee who know their Canadian history will recognize that it is one of the most important historical sites in the history of Canada. It is maintained at the present


time by the R.C.M.P. as a special place to raise their famous horses.
According to a letter which I have from the Minister of Justice, this application has been before this committee for a number of years. I would ask the minister whether he could give me the reason a decision has not yet been made in this matter. I am of the opinion that possibly because of pressure, if I may use that word, from the Department of Justice on behalf of the R.C.M.P. this matter has not been decided to this date. If there is a priority list I should like to know where this application stands on that list. I have had representations from that community, which is in my constituency. It lies in the southwest corner of Saskatchewan in an area known as the Cypress hills in the Maple Creek district. The site itself has natural beauty and is an attraction to tourists. Other speakers on this item have made reference to tourism, and I suggest to the minister that if he wants to gain tourist dollars for Canada this is one area which could be opened up to tourists.
Recently the chamber of commerce in Maple Creek has attempted to make representations to the government in connection with making this an historic site. The members of the chamber of commerce are wondering whether there is anything they can do as an organization to persuade the R.C.M.P. to permit visitors to the fort. I understand why the R.C.M.P. are reluctant to receive visitors at that site, because it is a nuisance. I do not suppose that the budget of the R.C.M.P. provides for looking after tourists, but when I see an item of $728,000 in the minister's estimates relating to this particular activity I do wonder what portion of that amount has been allocated to the province of Saskatchewan.
These people are not asking for very much. All they are asking for is a guide and possibly for some improvement to the road from Maple Creek to the site. I suggest to the minister that this is a less costly project than some of the others which have been suggested today. No request is made for swimming pools and such things-not that I want to detract from anything which another hon. member has said in that regard. However, it seems to me that the request of the chamber of commerce and the people from the Maple Creek area is legitimate, and does not involve high cost.
As I said before, the officials of the R.C.M.P., though not intentionally, are discouraging the opening up of this site, and

some of the excuses they have given in this respect cannot be accepted either by myself as the member representing that area or by the constituents I represent. The R.C.M.P. say there have no guides and there are no parking facilities. I realize that there are no guides, and possibly they have not the manpower to provide them; but as far as parking facilities are concerned, the area itself is vast with plenty of range land. I suggest that one of the greatest worries of the officials in that area is that a fire hazard could be created on this grazing land, but I think that could be overcome.
The suggestion of the chamber of commerce in the Maple Creek area is that if this site were in the United States there would be a four lane highway to and from the site, with hot dog stands all along the way. That is not what the chamber of commerce are requesting; they just want recognition of the site by the committee, a few dollars to provide a guide or two during the tourist season, and an improved road. This would not cost very much.
I wonder whether the minister would inform the committee if there has been any consultation on this matter between his department and the Department of Justice. My representations in the past have all been made to the Department of Justice because the R.C.M.P. come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Justice. However, I have now come to the point where, although I understand the position of the R.C.M.P. officials, I also feel it is time this site is recognized and is opened up to tourists. In the not too distant future I am sure this is going to come, and if the minister agrees with me I suggest that he talk to this committee and put this application high on the list.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw the minister's attention to an historic site known as Fort Cahiaque in my area, located in a very beautiful setting, approximately seven miles from Orillia and one half a mile off the trans-Canada highway. Professor Emerson of the University of Toronto has been doing considerable work in this area and has unearthed some very interesting objects. I was there one day when a heel of a shoe worn by a Frenchman approximately 250 years ago was unearthed. He is also outlining various buildings that existed in that area, including the longhouse. This is a beautiful setting which gradually slopes down into an area that 250 years ago was a lake but which
Supply-Northern Affairs today has gradually receded into a marsh. This area was once the location of one of the largest Indian villages in Ontario, and substantial evidence indicates that it was inhabited by approximately 10,000 Indians. In addition, Champlain stayed for some time in this area. Professor Emerson will be appearing before the board of historic sites later this year, and I ask the minister to give full consideration to his suggestions.
Considering the things we have done in the field of historic site development I think we have overlooked the outstanding contribution made by Champlain, who played a great part in the development of this country. When we consider the hardships that Champlain had to undergo, living in this area infested by mosquitoes, flies, and all sorts of diseases, I think it rates highly as an historic site and further consideration to the re-establishment of this site as an historic site, should be seriously considered, thereby helping to give Champlain his proper place in history in this area, and historically show the build-up of that area. As I say, this site is located near Orillia, one half mile off the trans-Canada highway in a beautifully wooded area in the township of Medonte.

maintopic: DISPOSITION OF OFFICE FURNITURE OF FIRST WOMAN MEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have two matters I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and his department, one of which concerns generally the province of Alberta and the other concerning my own constituency. The hon. members for Medicine Hat and Athabasca have already referred to the Wood Buffalo park which is located par-partially within the Northwest Territories, but I should like to draw the minister's attention to certain facts in greater detail relating to this park, because I think there is an urgent situation which requires a decision in respect of policy and action coming from that policy as soon as possible.
It is rather interesting to know the part of Alberta that is presently under the jurisdiction of the federal government. Of the total national parks area in Canada, Alberta presently provides 58.8 per cent, and this does not include the Wood Buffalo national park of which we are speaking, that portion in Alberta which is much larger than Prince Edward Island. In other words, this park is so large it exceeds the total national park areas in the rest of Canada. All the national parks in Canada including those in Alberta, other than the Wood Buffalo park, could be placed within the boundaries of the Alberta section of that park and there would still be 1,700 square miles of park area unoccupied.

Supply-Northern Affairs
These figures are even more interesting when based on population. Alberta has approximately one seventh of the population of Canada, and by comparison, Ontario with a high density population, has only 11.8 square miles of national park, while Alberta has 7,042 square miles, not including the Alberta section of the Wood Buffalo national park.
Mr. Chairman, we in Alberta are not against national parks as such because we feel they play a very important part in Canada and will play an even greater part in the future. However, in view of the size of the area now occupied by Wood Buffalo national park, withdrawn from the provincial administration and from natural resources development which would normally take place, this matter becomes extremely important. It is also interesting to note that 10 per cent of the total area of Alberta is taken up by national parks located within that province.
The suggestion made by the minister relating to some policy concerning the Wood Buffalo national park relating to an exchange of areas elsewhere in Alberta at least some of the area taken up by that park is a bit irrelevant. It appears to me that we tend to regard negotiations between the province and the federal government like negotiations with a foreign power, where there is a necessity to drive a hard bargain. I do not think there is any question of trading acre for acre involved, but a question of facing the facts concerned with the problem of working out a solution to the mutual benefit of both the federal and provincial governments, as well as the citizens of the province. Therefore I do not think the suggestion that has been made is realistic at all, particularly if the minister is suggesting that because the buffalo preserve was named as a park in 1922 by the government of that day, Alberta must now be penalized by the request that it provide a total alternate of 20,717 square miles of national parks. This is far out of proportion to the 4,933 square miles in the eight other provinces. I do not include Quebec in those figures because Quebec has not given land for national parks as such.
I believe it is the responsibility of the government to take a very hard second look at this whole matter, and to do so rather quickly.
I do not think any change in policy regarding Wood Buffalo national park need jeopardize the policy of the government in relation to other national parks. The transfer of natural resources to the provinces in 1930 prohibits federal development of the resources. In Wood Buffalo national park, at the present time the federal government is in the business of grant-


ing timber leases. More than ten million board feet of timber are being taken out of this park annually. Trap lines are being licensed, and fur is exported from the park area. The value in 1961-62, the latest figure I have, amounted to more than $77,000. The total production from commercial fishing during that same year amounted to something like 114,000 pounds.
When Wood Buffalo national park is returned to the province, as I think it should be, the many other resources there, waiting for development can be developed. This cannot be done at the present time because of the area being within a national park. That is why I believe it is urgent that the government take some action on this matter.
There are only a few areas within Wood Buffalo national park that lend themselves to park purposes, and I am thinking specifically of recreation facilities. Those areas are on the Slave river, on the Peace river and at Pine Point some 45 miles south of Fort Smith. These areas could well be protected under provincial park legislation. The provincial park could be extended on the east side of the Slave river and take in some of lake Athabasca, which extends beyond the present park boundaries. With rapid development foreseen in northeastern Alberta there is no reason at all why park facilities in this area could not be supplied by the provincial government.
In relation to the administration of the park, I would join with the hon. member for Athabasca in paying tribute to Mr. Ed Olsen, the superintendent of the park, because I think he has done an excellent job. He is truly interested in the preservation of the buffalo and is certainly willing to co-operate in every way, but the problem at hand goes far beyond what he can do as the one responsible for administration of the park, and falls squarely upon the department.
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister several important facts that have been brought before the government of Alberta by Mr. Fimrite, the member of the legislature representing the area concerned. I put this information before the minister not only because I believe it is most relevant, but also to indicate that for some time now the Alberta government have been trying to get some action from the federal government in relation to this park.
Forty-two years have passed since Wood Buffalo national park was established as a sanctuary for the last remaining herd of buffalo. I am taking this information from a speech made last April by Mr. Fimrite in the

Alberta legislature. The preservation of buffalo in the park has been a very successful project. One error that was made was that the buffalo preserve was established under the National Parks Act. Unfortunately the government at that time gave little thought to the development of the natural resources in the days to come. This area does not lend itself to national park purposes, and it certainly cannot be said to be a tourist attraction. So it is logical that the Wood Buffalo preserve should be taken out of park jurisdiction. To insist stubbornly that the area is a park because it was so named in 1922 certainly does not make it so at the present time. That is why it is necessary to look at the matter in the light of the present situation.
Mr. Fimrite went on to point out in his speech that there are a number of things required to make this area commercially important. One is the construction of the necessary transportation facilities in that northeastern part of Alberta. The building of roads is of prime importance to the development of the entire area. It is urgent that a road be built from Fort Smith to Peace Point on the Peace river continuing west to High Level on the Mackenzie highway, a distance of 285 miles. Certainly the federal government, particularly the parks branch, is not going to be interested in building that kind of highway.
Not only is transportation important to this general area, but there are great natural resources in the form of minerals located in the area. The Peace Point gypsum deposits are well known, and they need only to be removed from the authority of the national parks branch to excite the interest of developers. The relatively pure gypsum in these deposits is exposed in cliffs rising from the Peace river to a height of 100 feet. The thin overburden makes its mining a very economical matter. Conservative estimates of the gypsum deposits are that there are more than 100 million tons. This is of extreme importance to the developing industrial strength of Alberta and all western Canada.
There are other types of minerals in the park area whose existence exploration has revealed. Paleozoic outcroppings along the west bank of the Slave river indicate that there are large lead and zinc deposits similar to those at Pine Point, which were sufficient to warrant the building of a railway to that area. There is a possibility that petroleum will be discovered in the southwest portion of the park area. Uranium is an additional possibility. With the development of the Athabasca oil sands near Fort McMurray, cer-
Supply-Northern Affairs tainly a great deal of commercial and industrial activity is going to develop in the general area in which the park is located. The oil sands development is just beginning, because it will extend much farther north as well.
As I have already mentioned, there is a great deal of timber in the park area. The national parks branch has sold to private companies one and a half billion board feet of ripe timber. This was disposed of under a sanitation regulation that applied to national parks. Production is in excess of 10 million board feet per year at the present time. Because of the isolation of the area and the difficulty of access so far as transportation is concerned, this timber is producing a royalty of only $1 per thousand board feet. This is quite inequitable when compared with timber sales under provincial control, and the result is that the difference in policy creates quite a problem for the provincial government.
Among other national resources in the park is commercial fishing. The lake Claire waters within the present park boundaries are said to be capable of maintaining a flourishing goldeye fishery. The present catch has reached a maximum of 105,000 pounds annually. Fort Chipewyan immediately east of the park on lake Athabasca has been selected as one of the sites for the new provincial community development program, utilizing both the human and natural resources of the region, and commercial fishing is certainly a part of this program.
As far as the management of the buffalo herd is concerned, at the present time the herd is estimated to number over 20,000. A large number have migrated into the Northwest Territories. The anthrax infestation that the federal government is attempting to control is not limited to a region inside the park. Fortunately the disease is confined to a small area, and it may now be under control. However, the buffalo herd within the park is not free from disease. There is a high incidence of bovine tuberculosis as well as brucellosis among the herd, and the purpose of food supply for the Indians is not logical in the interests of public health. It seems to me it is quite a wrong argument that the management of these buffalo herds could be carried on equally well whether this area is a park area or not.
I am not going to spend more time talking about the development of certain recreational areas of community development programs, except to say again I believe these would fit into the provincial program, in the light of

Supply-Northern Affairs the location of the park, far better than under any national parks administration.
I would refer the minister to a press release which I am sure he has in his possession, issued by the provincial minister of lands and forests, Hon. Norman Willmore, ini Alberta, in regard to this, as early as December 1962. I draw to the minister's attention again that the provincial government has been trying for a long time to get action from the federal government, and the reasons the provincial government feels action should be taken on returning this area to it are listed as follows in Mr. Willmore's release:
1.	The development of the natural resources is clearly the responsibility of the provincial government and we believe this can be properly accomplished under the multiple use concept of resource management.
2.	The area does not lend itself either presently or in the future to development for national parks purposes.
3.	The government of Canada now holds a disproportionate amount of land in Alberta compared to the other provinces for various purposes, including national parks, which in all totals approximately 23,500 square miles. For example, in Ontario national parks comprise a total of 12 square miles, although this is the area of Canada which is most heavily populated.
4.	Alberta has developed an extensive system of provincial parks and recreational areas as well as establishing wilderness areas and we have reserved and designated many other areas of crown land for future development as our population grows.
Therefore the government of Alberta feels that the Wood Buffalo park area should be dealt with on the basis of return to the province rather than in the light of any exchange of lands. It is our belief that this proposal will serve the best interest of the people of Alberta and Canada as a whole.
I would urge the minister to set up a provincial-federal commission to deal with this matter and to lay out a policy and pursue the action that is necessary, and I urge him to do this immediately because this problem has gone on far too long already.
The second point I would like to refer to briefly concerns my own constituency, and specifically the historic site that centres on the original location of one of the earliest forts in western Canada, the fort named Fort Rocky Mountain House. This is one of the oldest and most important forts west of Manitoba. It was in existence long before forts such as Fort Edmonton. In fact as early as 1799 both the Northwest Company and the Hudson Bay Company operated forts at Rocky Mountain House. Basically they were fur trading forts, but also represented the very terminal point of the fur trading route at that time, coming eastward from the west,


with Rocky Mountain as the western boundary.
At the present time the North Saskatchewan river has deviated from its original course, to the extent that the entire site on which these forts were located is threatened with being washed out of existence into the river bed. The actual remains of the last fort to be built on this site are now just on the edge of the river bank. The old chimneys still stand, but within a matter of a few years they will be washed into the river. Already the tunnel that led down from the fort site to the river bank has been washed away, and it is urgent that the historic sites branch take a very close look at this particular site with the idea of preserving the remains of the original forts before they are completely destroyed.
I have had it checked by engineers in the area who tell me it is not a difficult problem. With modern equipment it would be a simple matter to clear out the original river channel, which is some several hundred yards to the south, so that the river could be diverted into its original channel instead of being allowed to erode away the north bank on which is located the fort ruins.
I have been concerned at a communication I received from the department relating to the historic basis of these old forts. In it it is pointed out that the chimneys and ruins which are now standing were built as late as 1864, and abandoned in 1875. There is some error in that information. We know there were several fort sites. Both the Hudson Bay and Northwest Companies had forts there and these forts were burned down at different times and rebuilt. There were several different sites, and the Glenbow foundation has done much work, and will do more archaeological work next year, digging up some of these older sites. However the fact remains that the present ruins go back much earlier than 1864, and moreover they are the last evidence of this historic site. Whether they were built in 1798 or 1825 really does not matter. They should be preserved, and I urge the minister to consider doing so because as we approach our centennial we are concerned about our early history and are trying to preserve as much of it as we can.
One of the proposed projects now before the centennial council is a re-enactment of the old fur trade convoys from the west to Montreal. The plans presently proposed would have a canoe convoy begin at Edmonton and

take some three months to travel over the old fur trade route. It would be much more true to history if this trip should begin back at Fort Rocky Mountain House, and I am sure those responsible for suggesting this project would agree to that, particularly if the department were to take the initiative and restore this site.
Further I would urge the minister to use his influence, so far as government policy is concerned relating to centennial projects, to support this convoy re-enactment that is projected as a centennial project. One of the ways in which he could do this is to pay very close attention to the historic sites along the route, not just the one at Rocky Mountain House but all the others as well. Since I became interested in this project I have come to realize how it could be one of the most practical ways of teaching history to all our young folk, and to our older folk who do not realize the tremendous wealth of history this country has. Canada has a dozen Davy Crocketts who could be the heroes of our young people at school as they study the early years of Canadian history. All this enters not only into the celebration of our centenary but is vital to the building of the national spirit we must have if Canada is to be the nation we all expect it will be.
I was most grateful that during the past summer the Minister of Public Works was able to take a couple of days off duty and travel over part of the ancient route which the great explorer and map maker, David Thompson, travelled nearly 200 years ago. We travelled together through the Rocky mountain pass known as the Howse pass which connects British Columbia with the fur trading route I was talking about-past Fort Rocky Mountain House and Fort Edmonton, through north Saskatchewan to lake Winnipegosis and then on through the Lake of the Woods to the great lakes, connecting with the Ottawa river system which flows right past parliament hill.
I am sure he shares with me a knowledge of the historical significance of this general area. In closing, I would urge the minister and the government to pay close attention to the responsibilities allocated to the department of northern affairs as they relate to the restoration and reconstruction of these important historical sites linked with the earliest days of Canadian history.

I deeply appreciate the consideration of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, but I am in great shape; I am not hungry. However, I do think it would be of advantage to the committee if I were to attempt at this point to deal with the considerable number of constructive contributions which have been made with respect to this item.
We are dealing now with the subject of national parks and historic sites. I think it is obvious to us that not only on this continent but everywhere in the world the preservation of outdoor spaces is of greater concern than it has ever been in the past. We, in Canada, with our relatively small population today, could do ourselves a great deal of good by studying public opinion in the United States in this regard. I do not think any single subject at the present time has been brought so forcefully to the attention of the people of the United States as this need to preserve places of recreation in the open air for future generations. Scientists, doctors and psychiatrists are now becoming authorities in telling us that we have to preserve our countryside-that the rapid pace at which most people live today has to find some compensation and that this is best provided by preserving intact our forests, our lakes and all those places outdoors where the public may go for recreation.
Before I resume my seat I intend, Mr. Chairman, to ask permission to have printed in Hansard a statement showing the attendance at our national parks over the past number of years. I was astonished to learn that it was only in 1947 that the total number of visitors to the national parks reached
8186	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs one million persons. Yet last year the attendance reached nine and a half million. The whole nature of the attendance at our parks has changed and we are confronted with a crisis inasmuch as we have a flood tide of people arriving by automobile who say: Where do I park the trailer; where is the camping ground; where do the tents go?- and so forth. We find there is a marked change in the nature of the traffic. As well as using motels, in the last two or three years people have been using sleeping bags, and roughing it-in comparative comfort, of course. There has been a great change in this regard. While we are doing our best to take care of the new demand in this direction we must remember that we have a responsibility for doing things now for generations which may be many hundreds of years away. Generally speaking, due to the interest in the United States where many hundreds of millions are now being called for by the President and by the secretary of the interior, it would seem to me we cannot lose by setting aside at the earliest possible moment as much land as we possibly can for this purpose.

maintopic: DISPOSITION OF OFFICE FURNITURE OF FIRST WOMAN MEMBER

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

We shall not go wrong in this regard because I am confident that the areas which we set aside will never depreciate in value. As a great natural resource they will increase in value, so we shall always be on the safe side. In addition, we shall be providing a requisite for the future.
I was very happy when, on Wednesday of this week, secretary of the interior Udall, in the President's plane, took over the loudspeaker to describe the beauties of the area we were crossing. He told us the point had been reached, now, at which the population of the United States felt it had a particular responsibility for the fantastic beauties of the Canadian region which the hon. member for Kootenay East represents, among others. I was delighted, too, to hear Mr. Udall admit that this was a matter of very great importance to Canada's balance of payments situation.
Bearing all these things in mind, I wish to thank members of this committee for the large number of constructive criticisms which have been made of the department and for the fine suggestions which have been put forward. I wish to dispense with the subject of historic sites by saying that members who have called the attention of the committee to particular historic sites in their areas can be assured that those sites will be given the
[Mr. Laing.)

keenest attention by the board on historic sites when it meets.
I wish to deal with a suggestion made by the hon. member for Edmonton West who is concerned, as we all are, with the orderly development of Banff and Jasper, particularly the service centres. We are concerned with the provision of a road through the park to the Yellowhead pass. We are completing as fast as we can the highway between Banff and Jasper and we shall be making a statement with respect to the Oberlander report, I think, on October 19, to the Jasper chamber of commerce. We will provide them with a copy, and the board of trade of Edmonton will also be provided with a copy so that they may study it and make suggestions to us when our ideas as to how the report can be implemented are announced in Jasper. We are of the opinion that the next great explosion of demand for service will be at Jasper and we are making strides as rapidly as we can to provide new facilities there to take care of the impending rush of people. The hon. member for Marquette dealt with historic sites, and what I said on this subject applies also to Fort Ellice. The hon. member for Grey-Bruce raised the matter of another national park in Ontario. What I said in this connection applies equally in his case. We find this difficulty, that under our act the provinces have to acquire the land and turn it over to us free of encumbrance. I will be dealing a little later with the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer, who says that Ontario has only 12 square miles of national parks and Alberta has 23,000 square miles. I can only suggest to him that I know how happy the province of Ontario would be today if it had one or two of those magnificent parks that are in the Rockies opposite the tremendous population of the United States; because if those parks were opposite the great cities of New York, Philadelphia, and so on, it is quite obvious what the first industry of Canada would be. It would be tourism, of course. But here is the difficulty; the provinces are required to turn over this property to us free of encumbrance. That is why I made the statement yesterday that the best

time for the establishment of a national park was yesterday morning, because the cost of these properties is going up all the time. At the present time we are working very, very closely with the province of Ontario in this connection. Our parks people are working harmoniously with the very excellent parks people of the province of Ontario in respect of the selection of a national park in that particular province.

I will now deal with his remarks with respect to Wood Buffalo park, as I will the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer.
Wood Buffalo park is an enormous park of some 17,000 square miles. I have been somewhat disappointed in that I thought it was a park of such enormous size that no matter what happened to our other national parks, some day we would be able to build a highway in there and this would take care of the overflow of all the parks visitors to Canada. Well, Mr. Chairman, it has not happened that way. This is an area with regard to which I have said that I think the space of time between unbearable insects and frost is too short. In addition to that, it seems to be awash with water in parts. It is not a park that will satisfy the requirements for the outdoors for a great number of Canadians. We are fully conscious of this. We are conscious, also-and this has been brought to our attention by the government of the province of Alberta-of the fact that the provincial government wants to get in there, take over the resources and exploit the park, at least in part. It appears to me-and I am going to face this point-that the government of the province of Alberta is a little more commercial than some other governments. That is not against them.

Supply-Northern Affairs visited the park last year. I have a great deal of admiration for our manager there, Mr. Webster; I think he is the best animal husbandry man we have. He is doing a splendid job and is supplying us with many thousands of bales of hay for other parks as well as for the animals there. There are 600 or 700 buffalo in one place there. I never saw a single buffalo when I visited the park. It was a hot day and they were all under the trees. I am quite sure that any visitor who went there on that day did not see a buffalo. These are plains buffalo, and I am sure they can stand the heat better than I. I suggest we should open up some space for them and let the public see a herd of some size.
There is trouble there with Astotin lake, I think it is called. This is a reedy, marshy lake. The hon. member for Vegreville and I were there on one occasion. We were not girl watching that day, but we saw people emerging from the lake with reeds hanging all over them, and so on. If we had a clear water lake there, it would be an extremely popular park. This is a practice which has been established in most other countries and we do not want to drop it for a number of reasons, one of the main reasons being that it produces over 30 per cent of our total revenue from the parks.
