speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Before I sit down I want to make an important statement in respect of national parks. We have for some time foreseen that we would have to make a statement on national parks policy in Canada. That policy has been established now and this is the first opportunity I have had to present it to the House of Commons. The announcement that the government has approved a policy for the national parks will be received with gratification, I am sure, by all members of the Commons and by the citizens of Canada.
A statement of policy on the preservation, development and administration of the national parks of Canada has recently been approved in principle by the government. This statement expresses the government's opinion on the best manner in which the parks can be best operated, developed and administered to serve the public interest.
There has been urgent need for at least three decades of a clearer, definite and firm statement of policy in this field. This need was recognized by the royal commission on government organization which recommended in its report that a complete review of national park policy be undertaken, and I quote:
.. .that operational patterns be developed which may best harmonize the twin objectives of meeting the recreational needs of the people and preserving the natural beauty and character of the environment.
Since 1930 the national parks have been administered under the provisions of the National Parks Act. This legislation, while durable and capable of being applied to most park administrative situations that will arise, was not designed as a full statement of policy. Section 4 of the National Parks Act defines the general purposes of the national parks as follows:
The parks are hereby dedicated to the people of Canada for their benefit, education and enjoyment, subject to the provisions of this act and the regulations, and such parks shall be maintained and made use of so as to leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations.
This section of the act provides the only broad guidance for the policies of the government for the public use of the parks and for their preservation. Knowledge of the intentions and principles behind the substance of this section has enabled the government to set out a policy for the national parks.
Park policy until now had been an unwritten policy, based on precedents and usage. Being unwritten, it was unavoidable that minor variations and inconsistencies appeared.


The statement of a unified, coherent and comprehensible national park policy became imperative with the greatly increased public use of the parks over the past several years. This volume of public use has attracted the attention of private enterprise and resulted in pressure for the development of recreation and entertainment facilities that, while unobjectionable in other places where the public meets, are unsuitable for national parks and, if allowed to expand unchecked, would destroy the parks' ability to contribute to the public benefit in the way they were intended.
The national parks of Canada have reached a critical stage in their development. Though it is a "quiet crisis", as my United States opposite number, Stewart L. Udall, has described it in his book of the same title, it is none the less a crisis deserving of public recognition and participation. Our national park system is the greatest single area that has been established for the outdoor recreational use of all of the people of Canada, and very great care must be taken to assure that it will not degenerate. National park policy cannot contribute to a solution of the crisis if it is based on one of the two extremes, maximum preservation on one hand, or maximum public use and development on the other. One would deprive the public of the benefits they receive from national parks; the other would destroy the special enjoyment and pleasure the public receives from lands kept in a near natural state. The objective of national park policy must be to help Canadians gain the greatest long term recreational benefits from their national parks and at the same time provide safeguards against excessive or unsuitable types of development and use.
I propose to explain briefly the main points of our policy for the national parks.
The traditional definition of national parks is confirmed as natural areas of nation-wide interest, in which are preserved for all time the most outstanding and unique natural features of Canada. These areas are preserved for the people of Canada for their benefit, education and enjoyment. By underlining this definition of the act we accept the view that national parks are not conventional parks or ordinary areas for outdoor recreation, but very special areas in which the finest examples of scenic beauty and natural wonders, both living and inanimate, are kept in their natural state for the people of Canada to see and marvel at, and to gain that mixed experience of understanding and inspiration that comes when one is confronted with a

physical expression of the finest of the Canadian scene.
Our understanding of the national parks as sanctuaries of nature where people can relax and enjoy themselves amid a natural environment precludes the exploitation of the natural resources for their commercial value. Canada is a land still rich in natural resources. We have not yet reached the desperate stage in our growth where every cubic yard of the land must be squeezed for whatever material potential it may have. To preserve as national parks lands that altogether make up little more than 1 per cent of our total land area is not a waste of natural resources, particularly when these lands together with their complete resources give our people the opportunity to find some solitude and freedom from care, to rediscover an easy relationship with nature, and to understand the beauty and significance of the natural features that express Canada's very individuality.
A quotation from a speech by Senator Clinton B. Anderson of New Mexico is relevant:
Wilderness is an anchor to windward. Knowing it is there we can also know that we are still a rich nation, tending to resources as we should- not a people in despair, searching the last nook and cranny of our land for a board of lumber, a barrel of oil, a blade of grass, or a tank of water.
The national parks have provided their benefits to the people of Canada only because the kinds of resource use that have scarred, destroyed, and diminished the scenic values of large areas of the country have not been allowed. Benefits of future generations will be even greater if the natural resources within the national parks remain in their natural state, untouched. Mining, lumbering, prospecting, commercial fishing, oil exploration and production, even hunting-these all would rob the people of Canada of all that is unique within the national parks and much of their attraction and beneficial purpose.
Development in a national park must be considered solely on the direct effect it will have on increasing the public's enjoyment and use of the national parks and on maintaining them as sanctuaries not only of nature but for nature. It does not follow that the government does not wish further development undertaken in the parks. Certainly adequate and appropriate developments are needed to enable the public to use the parks more and gain a better appreciation.
Where best to locate such development and the intensity of development permissible without the impairment of natural values are matters best decided by reference to a land
Supply-Northern A fairs zoning system. In any large area such as a national park, every point does not have the same scenic quality, the same potential for public use, or the same practical advantages for development. The areas that now remain as superb wilderness and are unlikely to be heavily used by the public in future because of their isolation from the routes followed by most visitors will be defined as wilderness zones. The type of development allowed there will be slight, mainly trails or canoe routes and primitive overnight shelter, the barest facilities that will allow access to these areas for the few park visitors who wish a true wilderness experience.
Other areas that are the objective of most park visitors and can be reached easily by extension of present road systems will be developed, but in a careful manner that will assure that all scenic points of interest are not obscured by buildings and parking lots and that the primitive natural beauty of the national park landscape remains to give the scenes depth and meaning.
Visitor service centres will be established in these heavily used areas. Like an urban shopping centre, a visitor services centre will be a grouping of all those services a park visitor wishes-a camp ground, motels, restaurant or coffee shop, gas station, information bureau, a store where supplies can be purchased. These will be located at less scenic locations, convenient to the main points of visitor concentration and yet close enough to scenic viewpoints and other places of interest that visitors can drive there quickly.
The establishment of visitor service centres in the national parks will inaugurate an orderly development pattern, faithful to the purpose of the parks. It will end the scattered development of services that is so irritating to park visitors, the situation where visitor services are scattered haphazardly along park roads and highways so that a visitor desiring a number of different services must make several stops and often drive farther than necessary. In terms of this policy, the present park townsites can be considered only as visitor services centres. Their only reason for being is that they provide essential services to visitors or services to the national parks and its staff.
The government does not intend that national parks attempt to meet every recreational need. To do so would destroy the special purpose they serve in allowing the public to enjoy nature and engage in activities that can be carried out enjoyably only in a natural environment. In future, only such activities

Supply-Northern Affairs as photography, sightseeing, hiking, swimming, riding, skiing, nature observation, fishing and boating will be encouraged by the national parks branch. There are many other types of entertainment and recreation Canadians like to engage in on holiday, but if these are unrelated to a national park and its special purpose and do not require a natural environment for their enjoyment they should be sought elsewhere. Because a national park generally has lots of space, attracts large numbers of people and is public land, many people think it can be developed to its maximum potential by allowing it to become a series of private or commercial resorts. This is a misunderstanding of the purpose of the national parks.
The policy we have adopted regards the national parks as a national asset protected by the national government, and a public service provided by the national government as a contribution to the health and happiness of the citizens. Therefore all basic facilities in the national parks, such as roads, trails, camp grounds, and public utilities, and the costs of administration and protection, are provided out of public funds rather than being paid entirely by the persons who use the parks.
Beyond that, all facilities needed to serve visitors are the responsibility of private enterprise to provide and operate. Commercial visitor services such as hotels, motels and service stations should be provided by the private sector of the economy. Where the public demands special facilities for their use, such as swimming pools, golf courses, marinas and fully serviced camp grounds, those who use these special facilities should pay charges that will at least cover the costs of operating and maintaining these facilities.
The policy regarding those who live and carry on business in the national parks is that they should enjoy no particular economic advantage or disadvantage because of their special place of residence or business. In general, they should be subject to the same financial responsibilities as those who live or carry on business elsewhere. This policy will be applied when charges, rentals and fees paid by national parks residents to the federal government are being reviewed.
A change in policy toward residence in national parks has long been required. In earlier times, when the national parks were not so heavily used nor so easily accessible as they are now, it was reasonable to allow persons to take up permanent or temporary residence, especially when they were regular
[Mr. LaingJ

park visitors whose place of work or primary point of residence was in the vicinity of a national park. Long term leases were granted to these individuals and buildings erected that served them as either permanent or summer homes. In some national parks, residential subdivisions were established to provide for the summer cottages of local park visitors or for the homes of persons who had no reason, other than a personal wish, to be living in a national park. The effect of this policy has been to give special benefits and advantages to individuals who were fortunate enough to live near a national park. National park land is public land that must be used for public park purposes, not for private residential development; it must be used in a way that clearly contributes to public enjoyment and service, not for the private benefit and convenience of individuals.
For this reason, we have adopted a policy that will eventually exclude private residential occupation of park land unless it is required by persons who provide services to the park and its visitors. No new uses of park land for summer homes, cottages, or permanent residence will be allowed unless it is clear that the permanent or temporary resident is providing some essential service to park visitors, or engaged in the administration, operation and protection of the national parks. Such improper occupation of park land by individuals as now exists will be eliminated gradually.
The over-all policy that we have adopted toward the national paries is aimed at achieving maximum public use and benefit consonant with the maximum conservation of the recreational resource. The growing use of the national parks by the public, the expanding demand for more outdoors recreation space that will serve both present and future generations, and the need to preserve with respect and in dignity all that expresses Canada's heritage demand a positive, clear and uniformly applicable policy.
The national parks policy of this government is intended to fulfil the aspirations the people of Canada have for their national parks. They have made it clear repeatedly that they are opposed to excessive commercial development and the types of use that make it difficult for the average family to enjoy a relaxing and restorative holiday amid natural surroundings. It is to the public of Canada as a whole that the national parks are dedicated, and it is to the public that the government is ultimately responsible for the

manner in which it manages the national parks.
As public property the national parks are worthy of the interest and attention of every citizen of Canada. All decisions affecting development by public or private enterprise in the parks must be governed by the national interest, and it is the national interest that our policy is intended to serve. Public understanding and support are necessary if the government is to continue its stewardship of the national parks under a policy that serves the national interest. I sincerely trust that not only every member of this committee will support in principle that policy we are following on the national parks, but also that every Canadian will assist in preserving his national heritage by understanding, responsible and appreciative use, and vigilance.
If hon. members desire to proceed with the debate on this particular item I would be entirely agreeable. I shall have a cup of coffee behind the curtains but I shall still be listening.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few brief remarks to make on this item, but for the sake of more orderly discussion if there are members who wish to discuss the minister's statement on national park policy I would be agreeable to let them precede me, so long as the item does not pass before I have a chance to speak again.

I am sure the minister is aware of the closing down of the last uranium mines in the Bancroft area. I am also certain he and other members of the cabinet are aware of the statement made by the Prime Minister, when speaking to the Bancroft chamber of commerce, that one of the first duties of the government, and particularly of the Department of Industry, would be to study means of developing some assistance to help the economy in that area. It is because of this I would ask the minister and his department to consider the developing of a natural geo-20220-519
Supply-Northern Affairs graphical asset, known as the Eagle Nest rock in Bancroft, as a park.
Several factors make this worthy of the minister's attention, both from the point of view of its value as a tourist attraction, and the practicability of its construction. The small park there, known as the York River park, is inadequate for the rapidly growing tourist industry of the region. Bancroft is the centre of a large and potentially rich tourist area, and I am certain that if the minister and his officials visited the area they would agree that this is a reasonable request and that an effort should be made to develop this natural tourist attraction centre.
The site is very accessible by two routes. The owners of the property are willing to sell it for this worth-while project. Recently the closing of the mines has insured an ample supply of labour in the area, and it is hardly necessary to suggest that the construction of such a park would be an important step in the readjustment of an area which has suffered from a slump in the mining industry.
I am also certain that such a project would reflect very favourably with the people of Bancroft, the district and the county as a whole. Before I take my seat I want to state that I am aware of the administration of parks in Ontario, but I would suggest that a generous contribution to such a project as I have outlined would be very helpful, would be appreciated, and would certainly coincide with the remarks made by the minister just a few minutes ago.

I am sure members of the committee were very interested to hear the minister's statement on new national parks policy. I agree with the principles outlined in that policy and I hope the minister will translate it into action at the earliest possible date.
If the minister has read previous debates on the estimates of his department he will know I have discussed the matter of national parks on previous occasions, and more particularly the development of another national park in Saskatchewan. The minister emphasized the terrific growth in the tourist industry, something I myself drew to the attention of this chamber on several previous occasions. In 1945 we had 1 million tourists and by 1963 this number has risen to 9J million. Canada is a veritable gem as a tourist attraction, and tourists who have travelled the world have told me they can see in Canada everything that is to be found anywhere else.

The tourist industry is now our third largest. The wood pulp and paper industry is our biggest, and agricultural exports hold second place. Last year we derived something like $500 million tourist income and I anticipate that in 1967, with the Canada expo in Montreal, it is quite possible tourist income will reach the billion dollar mark. Therefore anything we can do to develop this industry will be of the greatest importance to the national economy. I place such emphasis upon this, that in the past I have suggested we should consider the possibility of reorganizing this Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources so as to have a minister, or at least a deputy minister, with special responsibility for assisting the tourist industry in this country.
I believe the department should consider the development of another park in Saskatchewan. We have 18 national parks in Canada now, five of which are in the province of Alberta. I can understand the preference for Alberta because of the natural beauty of that province. But because of the part national parks play in the drive for income from tourism I think it is time we should consider providing another park in Saskatchewan. The one we have, the Prince Albert national park, is a very beautiful one, but it is some 500 miles north of the southern boundary of the province. It is interesting to note that in western Montana, North Dakota and western Minnesota-states which lie to the south of the border-the terrain is prairie land, similar to the prairie land of central Saskatchewan; there is little vegetation and little parkland. A large population which appreciates the beauty of Canada lives in these areas and many of these people hie north during the summertime to take advantage of what parkland we have in Saskatchewan. We find there is an ever increasing demand by tourists from the areas of the United States I have mentioned and also from areas of Saskatchewan adjacent to the constituency of Moose Mountain in which I live. This demand is overtaxing the resources of the provincial park of Moose Mountain. I have suggested in the past that the department should take a look at this area, an area 25 miles long by about 12 miles wide, to see whether it could be developed as a national park. The present parkland area could be developed still further by reforestation-plantations of evergreens, and so on.
I know there are problems which are likely to arise in connection with such a development. In the first place, the province of
[MT. South am.]
Saskatchewan has been responsible for a beautiful development of the section known as Moose Mountain provincial park. Naturally, the provincial government would have to turn over this area free of encumbrance to the federal government. I did take this matter up with the provincial government several years ago. At that time the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam was premier of the province. He seemed very interested in the project, or at least he led me to believe he was. I had an interview with the provincial minister of natural resources, Hon. Mr. Kuziak. He agreed with the principle of my suggestion and said it was worth looking into, but that is about as far as the matter got at that time.
There is another problem-the fact that the Indian reservation known as the White Bear reservation is situated in the southern part of this parkland area. The Indians, naturally, are jealous of their rights. On the other hand I believe they are well aware that anything by way of a national park development would lead to an improvement in their economy. At the present time they derive a great deal of benefit from tourists visiting the reservation from the Carlisle lake resort. I might say that in this mountainous area there are 11 or 12 lakes, three of major proportions -the Carlisle lake in the southern section, the Kenosee lake in the centre of the provincial park, and another, the Kennington, I believe it is called. So there are plenty of possibilities as far as the development of water recreation is concerned, and there would be no difficulty in providing for the beach areas which would need to be developed in national park. I think that any difficulty which might arise with the Indian population could be ironed out through the Indian affairs branch.
Another problem entering into this picture is that which arises because of the 99 year hay leases given to pioneer settlers in the early days in case of years of serious drought. One such year was 1961 when the possessors of these leases were allowed into the areas adjoining the Indian reserve to cut hay in marshes and sloughs. This privilege has, in times gone by, been of great importance when emergencies have arisen due to drought. But I believe this problem, too, could be overcome by compensatory measures.
Another problem arises because of the attitude of some of the pioneer settlers living around the lake shore of Carlisle lake. They are people who established their cottages many years ago. A large number of them are getting along in years. They like the privacy

and the quiet of the lake shore and are not enthusiastic about the prospects if the park is developed to a greater extent. However, the provincial government has already incorporated the village of Carlisle lake resort in order to develop, to some extent, the tourist potentiality in and around the lake, so I believe the animosity on the part of the village is gradually decreasing.
I mentioned the restriction of the geographical area as possibly presenting a difficulty. If the government saw fit to take it over as a single national park, I think the development of this area, 12 miles by 25 miles in extent, plus a concentrated planting of evergreens, with some Manitoba maple, would really enhance the attractiveness of the whole area. In the light of what the minister has said and in view of the statistics showing the increased demand for recreation facilities in parkland within reasonable proximity of centres of population, I think serious consideration should be given to the proposal I have outlined. Parents with young families do not like to travel 700 or 800 miles to a lake-shore if they can travel 200 miles or less. I think it is our responsibility to develop all the park areas we possibly can. I think it is an act pf providence that we should have this beautiful parkland area of Moose Mountain centred in the southern plains of Saskatchewan.
It is surprising, right now, the number of tourists from the United States who are coming into this area clamouring for accommodation to such an extent that the provincial government finds the existing facilities overtaxed. I believe that if this matter was investigated the provincial government might be ivilling, and indeed glad, to co-operate with the federal government if they decided this project was feasible. With the heavy demand ay the public for holiday facilities there are many places in Saskatchewan now, other than ;his area, that are clamouring for provincial ievelopment on not as large a scale as this, and the province might well divert some of ;he funds it has appropriated for further ievelopment of the Moose Mountain provincial park to some of these smaller projects, md spread the wealth, as it were, to other ireas of Saskatchewan. Mr. Chairman, those ire all the remarks I want to make as far is the development of a national park there s concerned.
I would now like to say a few words with [DOT]egard to historic national monuments. Dur-ng previous discussions under this particular tern I have mentioned the possibility of an listoric monument at Cannington manor. I 20220-5191
Supply-Northern Affairs refer to the old manor of Cannington north of the town of Manor, Saskatchewan. I might say that the provincial constituency of Cannington, in the province of Saskatchewan, was named after this landmark. This manor was developed back in the latter part of the eighteenth century and the turn of the nineteenth century. This manor house, or community, was organized and populated by a number of old country people. These people came from England, and the early settlers referred to this area as a wee bit of old England. When they set up the community there they built a very beautiful stone church, a beautiful school, and a three-storey manor house. They also built carriage houses, a blacksmith's shop, and they developed a racetrack. They even rode with the hounds. It was a real piece, as I say, of old England when it was in its heyday.
Some of these buildings are still in a relatively good state of preservation. I believe the school and church are still being used. But the manor house, due to its being such an old building, has fallen into a state of disrepair. It is in the centre of a beautiful piece of very rich farmland, but it is fenced off and is a little more isolated than people looking at it from a tourist attraction point of view like to see at the present time. The word has got around in that part of Saskatchewan, and in fact all over Canada, of this particular Cannington manor area and people at the present time during the summer season come down on highway No. 9 or through highway No. 16 and inquire of the people in the immediate area where they can get into this particular site. Visitors are coming to this area in quite large numbers, so much so that I believe the people occupying the land at the present time have had to put a lock on the gate in order to keep the tourists from over-running the buildings that are there and are not in a very good state of preservation.
I was very glad to notice in an article released by the provincial government three or four weeks ago that the premier of the province has recognized the significance of Cannington manor as an historic site and has allocated a certain amount of money for preserving some of the old foundations. This money has been allocated, not to repair or rebuild some of these buildings but at least to keep them in their present state of preservation. I was naturally very pleased to hear this, and the people in that particular area are very pleased about it. But I do not believe this is enough. I think the federal

Supply-Northern Affairs government should reconsider this manor as an historic site, particularly if they decide that the park area I have mentioned could be developed as a national park. I believe that a certain appropriation should be made by the historic sites board to assist the provincial government to maintain, repair or restore the Cannington manor area. If it were properly exploited by advertising and publicity, I am sure it would be one of the chief tourist attractions in that part of Canada. I would like the federal government and the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources to take these suggestions under consideration. I am sure that if they do, in the long run it will become the attraction I have suggested it could be.

Mr. Chairman, I know that the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre wishes to speak on another aspect of these estimates, and I shall not be very long in my remarks. I have only one complaint to make concerning the national parks, and I would join my colleague from Comox-Al-berni in putting forward a complaint about the $2 charge. It is not a very great charge, and I know it applies in all parks. Nevertheless, I do not like the principle of charging a fee for admission to public parks of any type. Perhaps a case can be made out for charging campsite fees. That is a different matter, and these fees should be collected separately. But I simply do not like the idea of paying for entrance to public parks, whether they be municipal, provincial or federal.
I listened to the minister's statement on parks policy generally, and I liked it. I think he has the right approach. I will be interested in reading it later in greater detail. I was also interested in the minister's comments concerning the Wood Buffalo park in Alberta. He mentioned the possibility of giving up that park, provided other lands are given in return. The minister mentioned that public opinion in Canada is against giving up even one acre of parkland or reducing the total amount of parkland by even one acre. He is quite correct in his assessment of public opinion, I am sure, in this regard. Even though Wood Buffalo park may not be a very good one for tourist development, I would certainly urge the minister to retain it until the government can get something in return. If they do not get something in return, retain it anyway. I see nothing wrong with keeping certain sections of land in this country in their completely natural state as nature parks; there is no reason why

every park has to be fully developed for tourist purposes. I think it is quite important in the whole scheme of things that certain areas should remain in their completely natural state.
The minister said he would like to see another national park between the Pacific coast and Banff. I realize some efforts were made in this direction. It seems to me that about a year ago the minister, on behalf of the government, made an offer to the province of British Columbia that if the Garibaldi provincial park, which is very close to the coast, with magnificent mountain scenery, were turned over to the federal government free of encumbrance, quite a large amount of money would be spent on its development. The government of British Columbia has refused this offer, and the reason for the refusal is what disturbs me. The government of British Columbia and the government of Alberta are not against the idea of limited exploitation of provincial parks. I deplore this attitude. I prefer the conservative or, if you like, the conservationist approach, that the parks should be used for tourist purposes only, with no exploitation whatever. This trend on the part of the government of British Columbia and the government of Alberta is, I think, a disturbing one.
Recently the Canadian Olympics committee met to choose a site for the winter Olympics of 1972. I believe Banff was chosen. Garibaldi park was advanced by a committee in British Columbia, and it really would be a very good site. It is very close to the main centre of the population of the province and to the main centres of population in the northwest states. However, it was not selected. I dc not think the government of British Columbia gave any assistance in this connection, because I feel that if the federal government had been able to acquire that park last year, when the offer was made and there was a commitment to spend a large amount of money, it might have had some influence on the choice of the site for the 1972 Olympics
The policy enunciated by the minister generally seemed to be an excellent one. The possibilities in the future for the development oi the national parks for the enjoyment of Canadians and for the amount of money they car earn by bringing in tourists is very great Although I think I could find some fault ir the details, in general I think at the presen' time the development policies of these park: are the right ones and are certainly preferabk to the attitudes which are taken by some o; the provincial governments.

Mr. Chairman, may I add a few words to those of the previous speaker. Coming from the city of Vancouver I am naturally most concerned with the development of the Garibaldi area. It has always been my understanding that the provincial government of British Columbia might be prepared to turn over Garibaldi to the federal government as a national park if they were allowed to withhold the right to natural resources findings and development, which I presume would be of a mineral character. In the last year in particular the provincial government has at long last been spending money developing access roads to Garibaldi and one company has been doing further development.
In view of the situation and the decision, which I imagine is conclusive, not to develop Garibaldi as a sports area within the next four years, could I ask the minister whether, in view of the most magnificent value of Garibaldi, in its being not only adjacent to Vancouver, Burnaby and New Westminster but also within an hour and a half drive from Seattle, Tacoma and Portland, there is a possibility of co-operation between the federal and provincial governments to develop what I am absolutely convinced would eventually become one of the most remarkable and fantastic recreational areas on the North American continent. Could I ask the minister whether there is a possibility of this type of planning, co-operation and development between the two governments?

Mr. Chairman, I am not unfamiliar with the Brighton beach area and of its situation in respect of Vancouver, but the hon. member will recall that we are representing a city that is only 77 years of age, yet with its suburbs today it has almost a million people. We will do very well if we do the things that he has suggested, and make commitments in this regard for the preservation of as many of these historical spots as we can. We in British Columbia have as our representative on the national sites board Dr. Margaret Ormsby, and I am sure the


hon. member will agree that we could not have a better person in this position. I certainly will see that this matter is referred to her. but we hesitate to give even a nudge in this regard, as the hon. member can rightly understand. If I can give half a nudge in this case I will do so.
You are referring now to the Brighton park, is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Yes. I am not unfamiliar with the history of the hon. gentleman's riding. It was not so many years ago that my father owned 20 acres on the top of capital hill for which he traded a stud horse. After paying taxes for about eight or ten years he gave it up, letting it go for taxes. My hon. friend talks about an illegitimate child and I cannot agree with him at all. I was up around Wall street the other day and noticed some very splendid homes, with a tremendous view.
I am sorry, I said this area was an illegitimate child of Vancouver as far as parks and recreational facilities were concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Of course I agree with him in that regard, but the hon. member only a few days ago received the agreement in respect of everything he has said of the mayor of the city of Vancouver-that Vancouver East had been neglected in the matter of parks. We are of course a federal administration, but as far as we possibly can we will work with the provincial and city parks authorities. This year we are contributing $20,000 to assist the development of the national-provincial parks association, which is doing a great deal and has a tremendous opportunity to combine the efforts of those people at the three government levels who are interested in the development of parks.

I should like to ask the minister one further question. Will the minister support a plan for a major recreational and athletic centre on Boundary road, which is the hub of the metropolitan area in the lower mainland?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: We will certainly be interested in co-operating in every way possible within our sphere.

Mr. Chairman, it seems that all our national parks are located in either Alberta or British Columbia and I am wondering whether there is any land left for anything else.
I should like to know whether there is any intention on the part of the government

to convert the property in the Gatineau hills, which at this moment comes under the jurisdiction of the national capital commission, into a national park under the jurisdiction of the department of northern affairs. I firmly believe that the eastern part of Canada is lacking in national parks, and in view of the close proximity of that area to this capital city I believe it should be converted in that way in order that at least the people in central Canada may enjoy it.
I believe that certain navigable lakes, such as lake St. Louis and the lake of Two Mountains surrounding the island of Montreal, should be considered for development as national park area to accommodate yachts and other craft, as well as beach facilities. In this area there is a population of nearly two million, although there is not one national park. These people on week ends travel to the Plattsburgh area around lake Champlain In the United States to enjoy the park facilities there. I should like the minister to seriously consider these two lake areas I have mentioned for the development of national parks so that the people of the congested Montreal area may enjoy the recreational facilities that could be established there.

Mr. Chairman, I only rise at this time because of the absence of my colleague for Cape Breton North and Victoria who is at this time at home on other Important business. I hope what I say is accurate because I have not had an opportunity to check it with the hon. member. Is the minister aware of the intention of his department to construct a clubhouse on the golf course at Cape Breton national park? I think that the need for a clubhouse is going to become most apparent very shortly. This golf course, the most beautiful in Canada, though some members may want to challenge that statement, is very much in need of such a clubhouse.
All hon. members are aware that in addition to the production by the C.B.C. this year the Shell Oil Company chose this course for one of its productions on their program "The Wonderful World of Golf". Without a doubt these programs will mean a tremendous boost to the tourist industry of Cape Breton. If the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria were here I am quite sure he would have something to say about the proposed clubhouse which I understand was in the planning stage, but was later cancelled. With the tremendous publicity we expect from these two television programs which will be shown later this year, the need for a club-
Supply-Northern Affairs house will become most apparent and I would ask the minister to keep this in mind.
I would also ask the minister to try to encourage more rapid development of the Louisburg fortress project. It will mean a great deal to the tourist industry of Cape Breton and the speeding up of the project would be of great advantage to our part of the country. There are a few more arguments I would like to put forward, but having regard to the fact that the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre yielded the floor for a moment about an hour ago and is probably still waiting to put his views on record I will not say any more at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity to ask the minister a few questions concerning the Akamina highway. As he comes from British Columbia I am sure he is familiar with this project which has been the subject of discussion not only by the present government but by the former government. I understand that the policy of both governments has been to stand behind the construction of the Akamina-Kishinena highway.
For the benefit of those who may not know where the proposed highway is located, may I say that it would start in the southwestern corner of Waterton lakes national park, extend into British Columbia about 18 miles and link up with another highway coming in from Montana. The governor of Montana and a posse of Montana officials came to Alberta some three years ago and meetings were held at Waterton Lakes to discuss the possibility of getting the governments concerned to construct this highway, which would be a tremendous asset to Waterton Lakes national park. It would permit people from the United States to make a circuit tour starting in Glacier national park in the United States and going through Waterton Lakes national park. If they desired to do so they could then visit other parts of western Canada.
The people of the United States immediately to the south of Waterton Lakes national park have asked our government to take action on this matter. Meetings have been called at the instigation particularly of the Waterton Lakes chamber of commerce. This organization, now headed by Mr. Craig, sponsored meetings as recently as the past summer to see if some action could not be obtained with regard to the construction of about one mile of the Akamina highway in Alberta and about 18 miles of the Kishinena highway in British Columbia.

Supply-Northern Affairs
I am sorry to say that the project has been held up because of certain federal-provincial snags. Let us get them out on the table and look at them. The federal appropriations which we are discussing today do not permit of the spending of any money for the construction of this highway and I can find no item in these estimates. No money appropriated by parliament for a highway under these estimates can be used to construct a highway or road outside of the boundaries of a national park.
If this highway is to be built, one way of doing it would be for the province of British Columbia to give a strip of land to the federal government. It would have to be possibly 160 feet wide and 18 miles long. A second solution would be for the provincial and federal governments to trade adjacent pieces of land which they now own. The province of British Columbia could give the federal government a piece of land in the southwestern corner of British Columbia so that it would then be federal territory, with the result that federal funds could be spent for the construction of the highway. In other words, the details with regard to who is to pay for the highway and how the project is to be worked out are still unresolved.
The result is that the people of Waterton Lakes and the people of the United States who have been co-operating with us so well are still wondering why the federal and provincial governments cannot get together and find a solution for the problem. I know the minister is fully cognizant of the problem and how serious the matter is to the people affected. I should like him to take this opportunity to explain to the people of Waterton Lakes and southern Alberta what is holding up the project. Why can he not get action on it?
I know that the former government sent representatives to Victoria and substantial progress was made, but I want to know from the present minister whether the project is in jeopardy. Has he given up on it? There is no item in the estimates to go forward with the project. I should like him to tell me, the Lethbridge chamber of commerce and the Waterton Lakes chamber of commerce, what the views of the government are and what plans he has for action to get the Akamina-Kishinena highway under way.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I certainly get no satisfaction out of saying it is the fault of the other government, but we have made it very clear to the province of British Columbia that if they will turn over to us the


Kishinena watershed, which is what we are discussing, free of all encumbrances it would then be our responsibility to see that the area was suitably developed. We would build the highway at once if that were done. However if the province should decide to construct its 18 miles of road we would at once find the funds to complete the one mile of road within Waterton Lakes national park. We have suggested to the government of the province of British Columbia that they turn over the watershed to us but they have not yet decided to do so.
As I say, I do not take any pleasure in saying it is somebody else's fault, but I want to assure the hon. member that we have done all we can to bring about action on this road. I was told in Lethbridge the other night of its importance not only to Waterton Lakes but to Lethbridge and the area as a whole, and I am quite certain that its importance to that area would be matched by its importance to the province of British Columbia if the road were completed.
I should like to respond to the statements of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier-Lasalle who pointed out that unfortunately there are no national parks in Quebec. We have had certain correspondence with Quebec and we have offered to co-operate in making surveys of certain areas. It has been suggested it might be a good thing if the Gatineau hills in Quebec were established as a national park, but I believe the Quebec department of resources would not think this would be an adequate area in which to create a national park. Quebec has a great number of very fine provincial parks, but I think there is now evidence that they would like to have a national park within the province because a great number of Quebec people travel to other parts of Canada, particularly to the maritimes.
I want to thank the hon. member for Cape Breton South for having, on behalf of the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria, said something about the park in Cape Breton. I agree with him that this is one of the most beautiful parks in Canada. The Cabot trail is simply magnificent, and I agree with everything the hon. member said with respect to the golf course.
Plans were drawn two years ago for rebuilding the clubhouse, but they were withdrawn because it was decided certain adjustments were necessary to the course itself, and at that time attendance at the course hardly justified the investment that was proposed. I agree that the magnificent adver-

tising we received this summer, and which will be shown on television this winter, will attract more people there, and that we have to get a new clubhouse very quickly. While provision for it is not included in the estimates for 1964-65 I am quite certain it will be coming along very quickly.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South also dealt with Louisburg, and I may say the progress there has made me very unhappy. It is very difficult to combine the work of archaeologists and builders at the same time, because an archaeologist does not do what a builder does. A builder is supposed to put down foundations and an archaeologist is supposed to undermine them. This is a tremendous fort, extending over an enormous area, and until we get the detail that is required, by excavation, it will be impossible for us to restore any part of it in a veritable manner. I think the people of Canada would not wish us to build anything unless it were a genuine reproduction of what had existed previously. In the meantime, we have spent a considerable amount of money and have not got a great deal to show for it. We expect to have a great deal more to show next year when a lot of work will be done above ground.
I might mention that there were 90,000 visitors to Louisburg this year as against
23,000	last year. This, together with the tens of thousands of artifacts discovered, dating back to 1732, has been of tremendous benefit to the tourist business and hence to the economy of the area.

Mr. Chairman, I yielded the floor so that all speeches dealing with parks could appear consecutively in Hansard, and now I would like to discuss something else which it may be thought has only local application but actually is of general public interest and applies to a certain extent to parkland development and preservation.
The hon. member for Athabasca referred to whooping cranes. I would like to deal briefly with the perennial problem of sandhill cranes and the efforts of the government to help farmers protect their crops from excessive damage by these birds who feed on grain on their way south to their wintering grounds. The minister may recall that I raised this question last year, when he gave a very descriptive answer, saying they were going to bash these birds down in Texas before they started flying north. Apparently they did not bash enough of them because 20220-52C-
Supply-Northern Affairs according to reports there are just as many birds this year as before.
I have not been home recently but I have read that for the first time in 47 years the authorities have declared an open season on the shooting of these birds. There was a ban on the shooting of them in other years, because of the danger of shooting whooping cranes, which occasionally come with these birds and land in the area around the north end of Last Mountain lake. I also understand from reports that daily checks are made to see if any danger has been caused to whooping cranes. The shooting season opened on September 1 and is to close tomorrow, September 19. I would like to know whether the minister can make any report on how this new policy of shooting sandhill cranes has worked out, and whether it will be continued, rather than reverting to the previous policy of using explosives to scare the birds off farm crops?
Last year I referred to the fact that there was a bird sanctuary established on the north end of Last Mountain lake. In fact this bird sanctuary was the first one established on the North American continent and was set up by the government of Sir John A. Macdonald in the 1890's. Last year I asked the minister what was the possibility of extending this sanctuary so that birds would flock into it and not bother farmers' crops so much. At that time he indicated his department was looking into the feasibility of extending the sanctuary, and I wonder if he has any statement on the progress made to date. I suggested it would be a good centennial project, and I still think so.
Dealing with whooping cranes, I wish to refer to a press release issued by the department on May 12, 1964, outlining what was called a co-operative Canadian-United States whooping crane management project. Announcement of this project was made jointly by the minister and by Stewart L. Udall, secretary of the United States department of the interior. It was indicated that under this new system of whooping crane management it might be possible to have an annual addition of 100 young whoopers to the total world population, which is now just around 32. The plan calls for a captive breeding stock of eight to ten birds being built up in the United States by incubating up to six eggs a year obtained by the Canadian wildlife service from the whooping crane nesting ground in Wood Buffalo park in the Northwest Territories. This is how I tie this in with the present estimates; there has been

Supply-Northern Affairs a great deal of discussion about Wood Buffalo national park. I should like to ask the minister whether he has any information with regard to a possible build-up of the number of whooping cranes as a result of this project.
There is one other subject I should like to bring up. We have heard a great deal of discussion about buffalo. In Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan, we have a local park where there is a herd of buffalo roaming in their natural habitat, as they did before the white man came. This is a great tourist attraction. Every year a large number of visitors come to this park. A plan is on foot now to develop a modern zoo in conjunction with this buffalo herd, and I hope the minister will give some consideration to any application which may reach him from Moose Jaw for assistance in establishing a modern zoo as an additional attraction to this buffalo park.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
In reply to the hon. member may I say we have had no reports about the incubation of whooping cranes. I know it takes 21 days for chickens to hatch; I do not know how long it takes a whooping crane. As to sandhill cranes, while we have sought the co-operation of the Americans we find we cannot instruct them to destroy sandhill cranes when the birds are down there; apparently it is not too much fun shooting them, because there seem to be more than ever this year. There has been a gradual rise in the numbers of these cranes and we are aware that unfortunately a great deal of damage has been done in several places in Saskatchewan.
I may say that the province has increased its contribution to Last Mountain lake area and have purchased more land for the protection of that particular sanctuary. In 1964 we agreed with the province that permits should be issued for the destruction of sandhill cranes, provided a competent biologist certified that no whooping cranes were in the vicinity at the time. I think this covers the point raised by the hon. member and I thank him for his intervention in the debate.

I have no intention of taking up a lot of time. I should like to bring it to the attention of the minister-and I have spoken to him personally about this as well as to his parliamentary secretary-that centenary year is only a stone's throw away. I know the department has worked toward this. I just wanted in my small way to add a little more pressure to that project, and the project is this-that we should have a series of national parks right across Canada. I do not think any project carried out by a depart -
CMr. Pascoe.l
ment of government would be of greater value to the generations coming along-to our grandsons and to their grandsons and granddaughters in the future. We are very fortunate today that we are able to go out and fish and see wildlife and take part in the shooting of it, if you want to say so. I think everyone recognizes that land in its natural state- and which not long ago we thought was so extensive that there was no need to worry about it-is fast disappearing.
I understand that the tourist industry is today ranking about second in Canada, bringing in about $600 million. Each year the importance of tourist revenue will become greater and it is obvious we must have facilities for our visitors as well as for ourselves. I would therefore like to impress upon the minister the need to make every effort to provide these facilities. I fully realize that this is not always easy, and that the department has to work with the various provincial governments. But I sincerely hope that the provinces, mindful of the needs of our people in the future, will in turn work together with the federal department of northern affairs so as to provide the parks that are needed.
Just one more thought. We have a number of parks which are not kept as they should be in respect to wildlife. I know there are enough places where we get sand kicked into our sandwiches and people spilling our coffee as they go by. We certainly do not want any more of them, though they have their place. I sincerely hope the department will see to it that there are always areas where no one will ever be allowed to build homes or put up commercial structures-areas left open for those who wish to explore, or paddle canoes or, if they happen to be in western Canada, pack their horses and wander freely among the beauties which this nation has to offer. I think we have a wonderful country and I think we should keep it. That is why I want to put these few thoughts on record.

I feel it is very encouraging that such great interest has been shown in this question of parks today. I think it is just as well a number of speakers have intervened between my own observations and those of my colleagues from the Vancouver lower mainland area who spoke earlier, urging the minister to take action with regard to an area with which he is himself perfectly familiar. Perhaps he has been reminded by some of those who intervened that he is also minister of national resources.

I certainly do not wish to indicate that I do not share the enthusiasm of the minister and of my colleagues from Vancouver with regard to the potentialities of Garibaldi park. I intervene again in this discussion only because of a brief exchange between myself and the minister on the question of park potential on Vancouver island. I think the minister will agree that whoever was responsible years ago at the provincial level in British Columbia for setting aside Garibaldi, and Strathcona park on Vancouver island, as park areas should be commended for his wisdom and foresight.
There seemed to be some confusion in the minister's mind as to just what area I was referring to when I suggested Vancouver island area. I think perhaps I should attempt to explain briefly my own conception of what might happen on Vancouver island. Strathcona provincial park was set aside in many thousands of acres in the very heartland of Vancouver island, with an eastern boundary that was set by the line of the original Esquimalt and Nanaimo railway land grant, and represents perhaps the most rugged and beautiful section of Vancouver island. Adjacent to that, but outside the boundary of the park is what is known as the Forbidden Plateau area in the vicinity of Courtenay in the Comox valley.
As the minister may know, there is a growing interest on the part of people on the west coast of Vancouver island in the development of a marine park on a large scale. As I see it, there exists the possibility for the development of a very major wilderness park area which would embrace some of the most beautiful mountain and seashore area to be found in Canada. There certainly is a growing interest and a growing concern among the residents of Vancouver island that action be taken toward a development of this kind, a development which would be completely in keeping with the policy for national parks which was outlined earlier to us by the minister.
I have been explaining to people on a number of occasions what the minister has said many times in this house, namely that the initiative in this matter must come from the provincial authorities of British Columbia. I have suggested to those who are particularly interested that they should seek to initiate an interest on the part of the provincial authorities in this matter. For some reason the government of the province of British Columbia up until now has certainly not displayed any great interest in the idea of na-20220-520J
Supply-Northern Affairs tional parks development in the coastal areas of the province. This to me is a matter of personal regret. It is not that I would suggest for a moment that in the minds of those who are responsible for parks administration in the province of British Columbia there is not a proper concern for the maintenance and development of the wilderness park idea; nevertheless, the fact remains that there is increasing pressure for the exploitation commercially of the particular heartland of Vancouver island which is included within the boundaries of the present Strathcona park.
I feel the time has come when there should be a reassessment and reappraisal of those boundaries so that a certain area which might be less desirable might be turned over to normal commercial development, but certain areas such as the Forbidden Plateau area and some of the seashore areas on the western coast of Vancouver island might be incorporated within the redrawn boundaries of a park. I believe that this natural wilderness heritage could be best preserved and protected if it were turned over to the national parks administration. I think it has been recognized that because it is a national administration with concern for our national heritage as a whole, it is therefore less vulnerable to the kind of pressures for commercial exploitation which can be put from time to time upon provincial governments.
I believe that the minister should be equally interested in the preservation of this area of Vancouver island as he has already indicated he is interested in the preservation of at least the best parts of the present provincial Garibaldi park. I should point out, for the benefit of members of the house who may not be familiar with the area, that this is a mountain area where mountains rise to the height of between 6,000 and 8,000 feet. There happens to be within it what I believe is the highest waterfall in Canada. I refer to Della falls, which drops some 1,443 feet from its mountain elevation down toward the drainage basin of Great Central lake. In the light of the general interest that has been shown today in the question of our national parks, and in the light of the statement the minister has made concerning parks policy, I wanted to put on the record as briefly as I could my own views in connection with the potentialities of this part of Vancouver island.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Chairman, in view of the remarks that have been made about the growth of our population and the increasing need to think of not only today but of tomorrow, and possibly of a century

Northern Affairs or more that lies ahead, I would like also to draw to the attention of the minister and the house the potentialities that lie within the large area of the mainland in the northeastern part of my constituency. Most people think of Comox-Alberni as being a Vancouver island constituency. Actually, however, in the number of acres there is probably as much of it on the mainland of the province of British Columbia as there is on Vancouver Island. In this almost unknown northeastern corner of Comox-Alberni lies the main mountain mass of the coast range of British Columbia. Within its area we have what in the days of my youth was known as Mystery mountain, which was explored by the Mundays who were mountaineers and with whom I am sure the minister is quite familiar. This is now known as mount Wad-dington, named after one of the early railway surveyors. This is a mountain that is higher than mount Robson.
There lie within this area icefields that are known to be much greater in extent than the more well known Columbia icefields in the Rocky mountains. I am not suggesting this is an area-because it is inaccessible at the present time-that should be the subject matter of any immediate plan for development, but I am suggesting that the people who are concerned with long range planning for the future and the preservation of wilderness areas in this country of ours should not overlook this tremendous wilderness area which now remains virtually untouched by man, except on some of its fringes along the coast line. I felt that in view of the line the discussion has taken I would like to take advantage of this particular opportunity, when we have had what to my mind has been a most facinat-ing discussion on the question of parks, with contributions from hon. members from all across this country, to point out what I consider to be some of our richest potential heritage in this field, which happens to lie within my own constituency.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks on our water resources. Canada has the largest bodies of fresh water in the world. We also have a great source of supply from the great lakes which is extremely important to industry, recreation and sanitary facilities. Industries and populations have settled in the great lakes area and this has created the problem of getting rid of the waste from industries as well as disposing of sewage. The international joint commission was formed, I believe, around 1910 and along with the provinces, states and municipalities has done a reasonably good job over the years. But this great resource of water is gradually being lost. I realize this matter has been referred to previously. It affects the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec as well as the states of Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, Ohio, New York, both directly and indirectly. It also affects the prairie provinces, in an indirect way.
At the present time the water levels are the lowest in 100 years, and while some people say that precipitation will bring some or all of it back I think that is foolish thinking. Anyone who looks at this situation will realize that today far more water is being used by industry, agriculture and the population in general, and it is ridiculous to say that precipitation will restore what is used, when it is being used far faster than in other years. To my mind precipitation only meets part of the problem.
It has been suggested that a committee of this house be set up to consider the matter but I think probably that is not good enough. This is an international affair and should be considered on an international basis rather than just by a committee of this house. It is not only a federal concern but provincial and international as well. Every avenue must be investigated. I think as far as the provinces and the federal government go they can deal with the tributaries and the water which runs into the great lakes. But when it comes to controlling the great lakes themselves, a committee appointed by this house would not be able to deal with that problem. If a committee is set up I would suggest to the minister that representatives from the provinces and the United States government
Supply-Northern Affairs sit in on the committee; otherwise the committee could not deal with the matter fully and do the work it should do as quickly a,s it should. First one reference and then another reference would be made until the matter reached the international just commission; at least that is the way I feel about it.
There are a few things we do know in this connection. I think we have controls on lake Superior-this may be rehashing matters which have been gone over before, but I think it worth recalling-and on lake Ontario, but broadly speaking we have no controls on lake Huron, lake Erie, or lake Michigan. Therefore any rise in the level of lake Superior would be very quickly dissipated in the vast reservoirs of lake Huron and lake Erie. As a matter of fact I think the minister prepared a paper on this subject for his parliamentary secretary which stated that in three years only 50 per cent of the water in lake Superidr would get down to the port of Montreal. '
There are certain facts which stand out here. If the control of water going out of the port of Montreal could be controlled by dam and lock, as it is partly controlled now in one branch of the river by stones piled across it as a stopper, we would find the run-off would be partly contained. I have reviewed this matter at some length and I cannot see any reason why it should not be done. I think the same efforts put in on lake Ontario and lake Huron would control water run-off, and if that water run-off were controlled I am sure there would be lots of time to investigate the other possibility of the grand canal project and other projects. I do not think there is much time on hand at present because in my area the water level this year was down very drastically, some said as much as five to six feet. This loss of water represented a great economic loss to the people running tourist establishments. One of the reasons the water was down this year was that not only was the water situation itself bad, but all of the frightening things said about it here and there which appeared in the press and elsewhere had an adverse effect too. I do not want to see this happen again next year. I want to see this problem well on the way to being solved before the next tourist season comes along. I want to see something definite done so that people can say we are working on the matter.
