Mr. Chairman, I am very interested in participating in the discussion of these estimates because they provide for water resources. I am speaking on behalf of a party which has been interested in the conservation and development of natural resources both on a federal and provincial scale ever since its formation. I have also put forward a federal-provincial program in this house repeatedly throughout the years urging the government to take action on some aspect of conservation of our resources whether lands, forests or waters. On behalf of the party I have moved a resolution in this house for a number of years urging a national-provincial conference to consider a national resources policy. I give credit to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle who, when the former government was in power took action which resulted in the conference held in Montreal, and the formation of the council of resources ministers. I think this was made easier for the government on that occasion, because prior to that the premier of Quebec had not been in favour of this program, and since Mr. Lesage became premier he has shown a willingness to consider such a conference.
Arising from that action, as I have said, was the establishment of the council of resource ministers who I think are going forward with this problem in the right way although very slowly, and I acknowledge all the difficulties there are in respect of ten provinces agreeing to an agenda and a pro-
[Mr. Rynard.l

cedure for an investigation of the development of any of our resources.
Today I wish to draw particular attention to the need for a national water policy and I know the minister is very interested in this subject. This is a subject in which I have been interested, as have my colleagues, for a good many years. I remember when we first brought this subject to the attention of the house in 1945, 1946 and 1947 at which time we were considered to be rather visionary in some respects. I remember the interest taken in respect of the question of conservation and development of our renewable resources immediately following the second world war, and the representations that were made to the government through members of the House of Commons by the Canadian federation of agriculture, trade union organizations located at various places in Canada, chambers of commerce and by numerous community groups, as well as scientific organizations such as the agricultural institute of Canada.
One resolution that was adopted and endorsed by some six of this type of organization, at a meeting of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, reads as follows:
Business and community interests in soil, forest, water conservation and land use are reflected in the chamber's policy declarations on agriculture and natural resources. In these declarations the chamber:-
(a)	Says loss of soil fertility, and erosion by wind and water are among the most important problems facing agriculture.
(b)	Urges government and business to extend educational programs on forest fire prevention, value and necessity of reforestation, and
(c)	Asks for national policy for control and development of nation's water resources.
Almost identical resolutions were adopted by various organizations including labour organizations from the prairie provinces which were particularly interested in the development of a water policy which would provide water for irrigation and other consumptive uses in the prairie provinces. At that time some of these representations and proposals were considered to be somewhat visionary. We hear that the same sort of suggestion today, that we should wait for 10, 15 or 20 years, but the problem grows more acute throughout the years.
I remember in 1954 speaking on this subject. I had moved for a number of years urging a federal-provincial conference on resources, and I recall that hon. members of all parties supported the principles of the resolution and the proposals. I remember particularly former prime minister St. Laurent stating that he supported the principles and admitted

that mistakes had been made here and there in the past. Prime minister St. Laurent said that on the over-all picture we were not doing too badly and that a good healthy warning had been sounded in respect of the depletion of Canada's resources, but that this should not induce too deep pessimism. As a matter of fact, the prime minister in my opinion was far too optimistic. We have done very little since that time and in some respects we have done some things to which I have taken strong exception, and of which there is growing awareness in this country.
I am very interested in the development of a national water policy, and have been following the minister's statements in this respect in this house, as well as statements made by his parliamentary secretary and other prominent members on the government side. I think it is about time that this government announced to the people of Canada a national water policy, indicating its immediate and long term objectives.
Recently I read a release of a speech made by Mr. John A. Turner, M.P., before the water level seminar sponsored by the Montreal port council at the Windsor hotel on June 30, 1964. There is quite a lot of good material in this speech. Quoting from page 2 Mr. Turner says:
It must be clear to all of us that the development of a national water management policy is a priority which must occupy us for the next generation. I want to say to you at the outset that Canada has had such a policy for many years but that, to my mind, it must be revised and sharpened.
While I agree with Mr. Turner's remarks in respect of the need for the development of a national water management policy, I cannot agree with his suggestion that we have had such a policy for many years and that it just needs to be revised and sharpened. I do not think we have had an over-all national water policy in any sense of the word, and certainly a great deal more has to be done than just revising and sharpening the policy we are supposed to have.
Later I read a news report of a speech by the parliamentary secretary to the minister made, I think, as proxy for the minister. The report is to be found in the Gazette of Saturday, September 12, and it is headed "Canada's Water Going Down the Drain?" I agree that it will be going down the Columbia pretty soon at a fast rate.
It has been for many years.

That is right, and we should do something to conserve some of it for our-
Supply-Northern Affairs selves. I am more interested in the needs of Alberta farmers apparently than is the leader of the Social Credit party. I presume this is a fairly factual report of the parliamentary secretary's speech. I took it for granted that it reflected the minister's approach and I was very pleased to read some of these observations. I am going to put some of them on the record so we will have them there for the future. Here is what it says:
The price which the public pays for confused policies, haphazard programs and ill planned projects is staggering.
I agree with that. Then it goes on to say:
It is paid in the form of: Floods, causing immense property damage, which could have been better controlled in many cases, avoided altogether in others.
That is quite correct.
Shipping, stranded or wrecked on a nation's waterways.
Another accurate statement.
The depletion, often to perilously low levels, of those secure supplies of fresh drinking water without which great cities cannot exist.
In my opinion that is an accurate statement.
The virtual destruction of once great commercial fisheries.
There is a lot of truth in that.
A pollution problem that is only beginning to be faced.
Mind you, this question has been dealt with in the house frequently since the end of the second world war. Yet it is admitted by the minister himself that we are only beginning to face the problem. The article continues:
Calamitously low water levels in great inland harbours built to accommodate the world's shipping.
The previous speaker dealt with that question and he is more informed than I am as to the need in this respect. It is obvious that this is one of the problems we face.
Abbreviated navigation seasons attributable to a hit and miss attack on Canada's winter ice problems.
An acute shortage of water for irrigation and other purposes in farm areas.
You should not think so from the way we have disposed of our water to the United States over long periods of time.
Spoilage of increasingly important recreational areas due to pollution or shortsighted drainage.
That is an increasing problem in eastern Canada and it is one that is beginning to raise its ugly head in some of our western river basins. It is one that is causing some concern to my constituents with respect to
8210	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs the Kootenay and Columbia rivers where some pollution has commenced. This problem cannot be solved by any small municipality or village affected, or by a provincial government and these villages. It will require a national water policy that will provide for the co-operation of all these levels of government if we are going to tackle this problem in the immediate future, and successfully.
The construction of costly public works which need not have been built at all or which have been planned so inadequately that they make necessary other remedial and expensive public works.
That has to do with river protection, breakwaters and things of that sort, and it is quite an acknowledgement after 22 years of Liberal rule and Liberal planning.
A costly and improvident contest for available water by the various classes of users-farmers, commercial fishermen, power companies, industry, lumber companies, transportation interests, governments and the general public-with scant regard for the modern concept of water as a multi-use resource to be handled for the benefit of all.
How true. The article continues:
A dangerous tendency to allow Canadian water resources to be diverted outside our borders on a first come first served basis, before Canada's own future requirements have been studied, let alone assured.
I am sure all members of this group will agree with that contention and observation. Then the parliamentary secretary went on to say:
Water remains Canada's most important natural resource. It is a resource which has always seemed plentiful and about which we Canadians have devoted altogether too little attention, except at times of crisis-flood or drought.
Then he goes on to deal with the various problems that face us in this respect. He deals with the various authorities that are involved, and I agree that it is an excellent analysis of the situation. He outlines all the various departments that have something to say about the administration of our water resources, and they are too many to mention. There are some two or three dozen at least. Then he goes on to say:
Even those agencies which come under a single department Jostle one another for pride of place in the sprawling federal bureaucracy and a bigger share of the departmental budget. They compete for the right to direct departmental thinking about water resources along the lines most advantageous to themselves.
Rival agencies from different departments behave on occasion in a less inhibited fashion, squabbling over methods and objectives, denouncing one another's reports and plans, purloining key personnel, blocking or stalling important projects assigned to other agencies in the hope that time may produce


a beneficial change. This buccaneering approach to the nation's water problems is not universal. It is, however, all too common.
The jungle-like atmosphere which prevails in the water resource field is attributable less to the agencies themselves than to the unsystem-like system under which they are required to perform. Operating under the watchful eye of no single department, acknowledging the over-all authority of no single minister, exposed to no coherent policy, the agencies are scarcely encouraged to work together co-ordinating their efforts. With authority fragmented from top to bottom the ordinary decision making machinery is short circuited. The consequences are serious.
Then he goes on to deal with a number of consequences of this fragmentation of administration. I am very glad to see that brought out in the open because the members of this group have dealt with that aspect of the question while not being as well or as fully informed as the parliamentary secretary. This is a problem that has to be faced if we are going to deal with it successfully and give effect to a national water policy.
In view of this speech by the parliamentary secretary I trust this is the line along which the minister is thinking. We are very glad to see this because first of all we must have a purpose and objective, we have got to have a policy and then we must have an administration that can give it effect instead of having our water resources dealt with by so many agencies. I have had several experiences in my own constituency where the conflict between various departments with some limited jurisdiction over certain aspects of our water problems was very obvious. That is that.
I was also very pleased to note that there are others who are concerned about this matter. The Kingston Whig-Standard of Tuesday, September 15 last contained a very interesting editorial which I wish to bring to the minister's attention because I trust it will stiffen his back so that he will stand up for Canada in the days ahead. It is entitled "The Columbia Money Game", and the last paragraph reads in part as follows:
The real winners-as we predicted years ago- are the successful Americans who talked this country into handing over those sovereign rights for a paltry few million dollars-

-which have not left the U.S.-and Premier Bennett, who can hardly wait to start collecting his 5 per cent.
The hon. member for Kootenay East does not like to be reminded about this but I could not resist mentioning-

-the observations of this very intelligent editorial writer. I read the report of the excellent speech of the minister's parliamentary secretary and I thought that we were on the road to a policy. Then I got a manuscript of a speech delivered by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister. It was entitled "The Great Northern Water Plan", and was a luncheon address delivered at the 52nd general conference of the Pacific northwest trade association at Prince George, B.C. on September 14, 1964. Possibly the parliamentary secretary was affected by the spirit and mood of the gathering, because a great number of the people in attendance at this luncheon were United States businessmen interested in the development of Washington, Oregon, Montana, Idaho and other states in the northwest.
I forgot to mention that while I was very critical in previous statements-at least I asked certain questions previously with respect to the superintendent in one of the minister's parks, at the request of some of his friends-I do want to emphasize the fact that, with the exception of two former deputy ministers who are widely condemned, and not including Major General Young, who is a real man, I have heard nothing but commendation for the officials of the minister's department, and I was very sorry the estimates for national parks were passed without some reference to the good work being done by the wildlife branch.
I judge the parliamentary secretary's speech was delivered on the basis of the recently announced policy of Premier Bennett in B.C., and to meet the feelings of the persons who were listening. I want to quote some paragraphs from his speech and contrast them with the speech I previously quoted. He began:
Mr. Chairman, ladies and gentlemen-
I can imagine the young man standing up and saying that.
Today I want to talk about water. I want to talk about water resource development on a grand scale. I also want you to look ahead 50 or even 100 years. By then, we will be diverting our northern rivers southward. Advancing technology will help us to skim off their flood waters in order to meet the urgent requirements of people who live in the south.
Is this not what we were foretelling when Premier Bennett proposed taking over the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, and when some hydro officials in B.C. are look-
Supply-Northern Affairs ing forward to the development of the various rivers in the north? He went on:
Man's inventiveness is, no doubt, our greatest resource. It is turning mountains of granite into fuel for our atomic furnaces. It is erasing the fear from our minds that mankind will ultimately run out of energy. It is putting more food on our tables. So mass starvation is no longer the spectre that it once was.
Replying to questions in the committee on external affairs the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that regardless of the foreign aid given by Canada and other countries, to India and similar countries, the gap between their standard of living and ours was still widening. But here the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister talks about-
-erasing the fear from our minds that mankind will ultimately run out of energy. It is putting more food on our tables-[DOT]
-and so on. He continued:
Even the metals are becoming cheaper to produce with each passing decade. So why worry, unduly, about water? It, too, can be used over and over again or drawn from alternative sources to meet our expanding needs.
I want to draw the minister's attention to the conflict in philosophy between his speech and the one given by the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister. Mind you, we are used to him shifting his ground on occasion. He was very critical of the Columbia river treaty during the election. Later he supported it then he disappeared from the house when the vote was taken. One can ask, where does he stand? At page 4 of his speech he said:
Nor do I under-rate the difficulties of repatriating our water supplies. Once committed, we may never be able to terminate exports of certain Canadian waters to the United States. We must face this prospect and face it head on. Treaty arrangements will be necessary. They must be spelled out in the clearest possible terms. Otherwise we will be involved in misunderstandings which will be harmful to our international relations for generations to come.
As a North American I cannot, however, ignore the fact that the demand for water is rising and rising rapidly. We are told by your federal experts-
And this indicates he was talking to a United States audience.
-that U.S. requirements will have risen fourfold between now and the end of the century. Billions of dollars will have to be spent on water diversion and water recovery projects of one kind or another.. . .You, in other words, will be prepared to pay and pay heavily for new sources of supply.
You see-buy Canadian water.
Under these circumstances, we in Canada, are unlikely to let our great northern rivers flow forever and without interruption to the sea.
What should we be going now? I suggest we should be already thinking in terms of a great
8212	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs
northern water plan. Its concept is simple. Its execution, I believe, is inevitable. In effect, we will be turning our northern rivers around. Some part of their flood waters will be diverted southward- southward and eastward-to meet the more urgent needs of Canadians and Americans in the big cities and towns whose growth would otherwise be hindered for lack of this vital, life giving resource.
Think, if you will, of a great continental water plan. Project your mind ahead to the time when the consumptive uses of water-irrigation, domestic and industrial-have become even more important than the generation of hydroelectric power.
I just want to quote another paragraph or two which appeared to me most interesting. Toward the end of his address he said:
There is only one place for the water to come from; that is the north. The flood crests of our northern rivers perform no useful function at the present time. They can, and I believe eventually will, be skimmed off and directed to the regions of greatest need.
Engineering studies are required. Means of financing must be explored. And finally a treaty or treaties may have to be negotiated between Canada and the United States.
Here he is suggesting a treaty should be negotiated between Canada and the United States before he is even thinking of ways and means of getting this water out to the people in B.C. who require it to the Okanagan, and to the people who require it on the prairies and in other parts of the country. He went on:
All of this will take time. But we must start somewhere. I therefore urge that more of us turn our eyes northward; that we plan against a background which is essentially continental in scope.
Not Canadian in scope, mind you-continental in scope; and this fits completely into the ideas advanced by some of these people in the United States in recent weeks in regard to the continental development of water. It is all right to have a continental scope so long as our government makes certain that all future requirements of water by the Canadian people, requirements for all its various consumptive purposes, are protected and met. That is the first consideration and until we have done that we are not in a position to deal with any other nation in respect to the sale of surplus water. I suggest the minister has a better approach to this problem than the parliamentary secretary, who went on to say:
An exchange scheme linking Alaska with the United States has a great deal to recommend it. Canada, besides providing a land bridge joining Alaska with the other states, may also be able to dispose of some of its cyclical water surplus for lump sum payments made in advance to cover the work involved.
This is the Columbia river treaty over again -we will give you some money to build the


dams so long as you sell us all the water we require in the future.
The entire plan may take decades to put into effect. Certain projects-elements of an over-all plan-may however be completed in your lifetime and mine.
Then he went on to deal with the Parsons plan and said:
I know that Washington has launched various investigations, several of which look to the possibility of importing water from Canada. The Parsons plan (known also as the North American water and power alliance) is now before the U.S. senate committee on public works. The question of low water levels on the great lakes has been turned over to the international joint commission.
Then he went on to deal with the necessity for planning and so on.
There is no doubt about it, there is a conflict of philosophy between the minister's approach to this question and the approach taken by the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister. I have drawn this matter to the attention of the minister and of the committee because of the great concern we feel about it. We are not opposed to co-operation with other countries as long as it is on a basis of equity, as long as the Canadian government protects, first of all, the needs of this and future generations with regard to water for irrigation and other consumptive purposes, and any other needs which may develop. Water, as the minister himself said a week or two ago, has become our most valuable national resource.
On behalf of the members of this party I urge the minister to develop a national water policy in co-operation with the provincial governments so as to provide Canadian water for Canadian soil, Canadian water for Canadian power requirements, Canadian water for all other consumptive purposes. In doing so he will provide jobs for Canadians not only in the limited period of the construction of dams but for generations to come.

The provisions of the Canada Water Conservation Act are, of course, available to all the provinces. The use of this act appears to have been largely restricted to Ontario, and indeed to metropolitan Toronto. Within ten or 12 miles of the centre of that great city they are providing park lands and areas for recreation which are unprecedented anywhere. However this legislation is available to other provinces, and I understand we are now about to receive an application from the province of British Columbia in respect to the north shore where some flood damage has occurred. I believe British Columbia will apply for assistance in raising the levels of the dikes in the Fraser valley to the extent of about $4.9 million in all. private concerns towards the progress and development of designated areas.

Mr. Chairman, I would like now to deal with another matter.
As you probably know, the general economic survey of the Gaspe peninsula, requested by a number of groups in the area, shows that there is an urgent need to do everything possible in order to take advantage of our resources.

Some ten years ago it was claimed that there was no room left in the Gaspe peninsula to build wharves and develop harbours. At that time, Mr. Leopold Langlois, former member for Gaspe, in co-operation with the Department of Public Works, had met all the requests of the local authorities. Today most of those commercial wharves can no longer meet present needs. Those wharves were built for shallow-draught ships, such as schooners used for carrying wood and freight. The wharf needed no more than 15 feet of water.
Since the deepening of the St. Lawrence small boats are not being built and the tonnage of new ships will increase year by year. Therefore, the Department of Public Works has to spend large sums of money to meet the wharf requirements in eastern Canada

because everything has to be done over again, such is the case in my region.
Mr. Chairman, may I call the attention of the Minister of Public Works to some letters I have received?
Quite recently, on August 31, 1964, I received the following letter from the Frank Byrne Pulp wood Inc. company:
If my memory is good, I wrote to you last year to ask whether it was possible to get much needed improvements at the Madeleine and Marsoui wharves, in the Gaspe peninsula.
From Matane to Cloridorme, I buy several thousand cords of pulpwood and we are at the point where none of the companies with which we do business want to use those wharves. I do not request wharves for sea-going ships, but merely a sort of shelter which engineers could no doubt build to serve our purpose, at a reasonable price. We are ready to indicate to your engineers the sites and what would be required for the boats. The matter of schooners is not taken into account, because they do not use them much, although I am convinced that they would be pleased to use those wharves.

-our company here in Marsoui paid more than $600,000 in salaries in 1963, and we expect that this figure will exceed $1 million in 1964 and during the coming years.

Mr. Chairman, last year the sawmills of north Gaspe almost had to close down as they were unable to get boats to ship their lumber overseas, for lack of adequate and protected wharves. Some insurance companies now refuse to take the risk of ships stopping alongside some wharves such as in Cap Chat.
Last year, thanks to the co-operation of the Minister of Transport, a tugboat was ordered to stand by to protect the ships.
In order to help S.S. M.V. Dadmar, the James Richardson Company, of Cap Chat, had to pay $3,750 to the Foundation Marine Ltd., of Halifax, for the services of the tugboat Foundation Valour.
Supply-Public Works
It is hardly reasonable that in 1964 a private firm should have to disburse any amount for tugboat services, because of the inadequacy of the wharves.
At Cap Chat, the wharf runs out directly into the gulf; it has no protection whatever against winds and high seas.
The result is that it is impossible to load heavy tonnage boats on days of strong winds, which occur frequently in that area. The maximum draught is 20 feet, which does not favour deep-draught traffic toward the Atlantic.
At Cap Chat, Ste. Anne des Monts, Marsoui, Madeleine, Grande Vallee and other important municipalities of the coast, the Department of Public Works will have to consider heavy expenditures during the forthcoming years for the improvement of wharves so as to retain in the area the few industries which are operating at present.
The situation is nearly the same in the fishing harbours. Most of these ports were built for little fishing boats 20 to 35 feet long, and the fishing boats are now nearly 80 feet long.
In the last few years the department has co-operated closely with the fishermen's union and the Quebec united fishermen in order to meet the present situation as well as possible and so that the structures which are being built meet future needs of the fishing industry.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for the active part he played in the negotiations with the Quebec government, in conjunction with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), concerning the project of renovating highway No. 6 in north Gaspe for which the government will have to contribute $13 million.
I wish success and good health to the minister and I wish he could accompany his officials in Mont Joli and visit the eastern development board.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say but a few words about one very important aspect of the minister's departmental operations, as they bear on the province I have the honour to represent. Over the last seven or eight years there has been a good deal of talk about the causeway which the previous government indicated would be built between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. I should like to report to the minister on something of which he should be aware, and that is that there is considerable disquiet and unrest in Prince Edward Island over the lack of a definitive and comprehensive statement on this particular and very

Supply-Public Works important project. As the minister well knows, alert historian that he is, the very nub of the relations between our little province and the dominion has been communications and transportation. This was at the forefront of the negotiations which brought in our province in 1873, and we have constantly sought and pleaded for continuous and efficient communication with the mainland.
We were quite elated, Mr. Chairman, when with the advance of technology and engineering skill we reached the stage where a continuous land link with the mainland was possible. We were all the more thrilled when the government of the day declared that that which was possible, a causeway, would be constructed.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Well, all right.

It is just a brief one. I wonder if the hon. member could tell whether the people of Prince Edward Island are convineed that a causeway would be a good thing? Would this not destroy the uniqueness and charm of that province, flooding the island with hundreds and thousands of motor vehicles coming over from the mainland every year? Is he not better off the way he is now?

I can only say that I should have liked the company of my hon. friend last Sunday when I made a very fast trip from Sackville, driving far too fast, in order to get to the ferry terminal, and then discovered I had to sit there and wait, owing to insufficient room, while three boats left. I thought at that time that I would have loved to have with me some of the people who think that it is a charming thing to have the boats. We have arranged, with our Prince Edward Island canniness, that when the causeway is built we will still have the ferry service between Wood Island and Nova Scotia, and anyone who wants a sail can carry on his trip. However I do appreciate the remarks of the hon. and learned member.
Let me say in all seriousness that we recognize the role of the tourist, and as I said this morning this is the most expandable and rapidly expanding industry we have. But more important than that is the primary producer, the farmer and the fisherman, and his ability to get his goods rapidly to market by a sure and certain communication. The means the causeway would provide I think vastly transcends the charm of the boat sail.

We are nautical people and we love boats, but we are also very hospitable people and not afraid of being overwhelmed. We welcome strangers, be they from British Columbia, be they Liberals, Social Crediters or even members of the N.D.P., and over the years I do not think there has been any indication that we have lost our own cultural uniqueness. I do not fear that at all, any more than Cape Breton has reason to worry about losing its individuality. I would not like the minister to entertain any suggestion that he is protecting Prince Edward Island's culture by not moving forward as rapidly as possible with the causeway.
When the former government was in office we were delighted by the forthright statement of the leader of that government that thecauseway would be built. We are looking to this government for a reassertion of the same positive and definite intention. I am not going to say that they have welshed on this arrangement, or that they have backtracked, because I make no accusations that I cannot back up, but I think they would be in a much better position, vis-a-vis our people, if they would forthrightly indicate their intention.
Another thing which has caused us much concern is the seeming veil of secrecy which surrounds the reports which have been elaborately and, I may say, Mr. Chairman, expensively prepared. I can recall when the member for Bonavista-Twillingate used to criticize the then minister of public works for not divulging, not indicating, not tabling and not presenting a report at that time; but the report then had not been completed. As I understand the situation now, the report has been completed and we know that it is vast, exhaustive and tremendous, but still we do not know what is in it. Considering the importance of this to Prince Edward Island, considering the vast expenditure of taxpayers' money, surely it is incumbent upon the government to indicate in considerable detail, whether replete with technical information or not, what is the present thinking of the government.
We are constantly reading statements by the Solicitor General to the effect that consideration is being given to building the structure without rails. We would like to know whether the government has had anyone investigate the feasibility of interprovincial travel by means other than rails, how much Price Edward Island would suffer if the railway was completely abandoned, and what would be the costs.

We would be interested to know the government's reaction to the suggestion-indeed, the positive offer-by a very prominent and reputable private organization, headed I believe by Mr. A. D. Margison, a man of wide repute, in reference to the building of this project. This is a tremendous offer. What is the government doing about it?
I have heard about mysterious meetings of the Minister of Transport, the Solicitor General and the provincial minister of highways. I did not hear of these meetings from the minister of highways but from someone who happened to be at the airport at Charlottetown. Surely this is not a matter of high secrecy, but a matter of tremendous public importance to the people in my province. We are interested in receiving the fullest possible information, and we wonder how much investigation has been carried out in reference to a similar project at Chesapeake bay. Have the people who made that feasibility report been consulted? Have other private offers been made other than that made by Mr. Margison?
In other words, to put it very simply, I say to the minister, Mr. Chairman, that we should like him to indicate to this house and to the province just exactly what is going on. It is not for me to comment on the relationship among ministers of the cabinet, but I am a little surprised that his name does not figure more prominently in discussions, in view of the fact that it is his department that is responsible. He is a minister with a tremendous reputation and we know of his concern for all parts of Canada. We wonder why he is not more prominently in the picture and mentioned perhaps more frequently than the Minister of Transport.
It is in respect of some of these matters that we want to know the government's stand and attitude towards offers that have been made. We want to know what the thinking is in reference to rail traffic. Has the government decided that it cannot and will not build a causeway with rails? Let the people know the answer so that they can make a judgment. This matter has been under consideration for a long time and is of tremendous importance. It is one of the great challenging public works projects of our time. I want to co-operate with the minister in every possible way and it would not injure my pride at all if the whole thing were built and completed as soon as possible-I was going to say, even while this party was in power, but I suppose even modern technology is not that rapid. We are not inter-
Supply-Public Works ested in political partisanship in respect of this matter. We want to wish the minister well and assist him in any way possible because this is a very important matter. I suggest to him, and even advise him, to be a little more forthcoming with information for the people of Canada generally, and particularly those people in Prince Edward Island who are especially concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I made my general observations when the minister's estimates were before the house but I should like to ask a question or two on this occasion.
I suppose the minister is aware of the fact that in the Arrow lakes region, owing to the proposed building of the High Arrow dam-I hope they do not even find the foundation satisfactory-there will be 12 or 13 wharves displaced, which are very important and serve various communities at this time. Some of these communities will be flooded completely and others only partially. Can the minister indicate to the house whether any survey has been made by his department of the needs for wharves after the High Arrow dam is complete? Will there be a relocation of various wharves, or the building of new wharves after this dam has been constructed, and has there been any co-operation whatsoever between the B.C. hydro power authority and the minister's department in respect of planning to meet these needs in the days ahead? If there has been a survey, who will be responsible for the cost of these new wharves, the minister's department or the B.C. hydro power authority? I would appreciate very much the minister letting the house know what has been done to date in this respect, and what the department intends to do in the way of investigation, and at whose expense.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to be repetitive but I should like to say that I associate myself with the remarks that have been made by my colleague, the other hon. member for Queen's, Prince Edward Island.
In respect of the remarks made by that hon. member, who just asked a question, I am under the impression, as I think all Prince Edward Islanders are, that this government intends to honour the commitment of the previous government that a causeway would be built, and that there is no longer any question as to a decision in that regard, but only a question as to how quickly, and what type of causeway it will be.

Supply-Public Works
I should like to point out that under the present system as traffic increases it is carried at a deficit, and the cost to the federal government of providing this service increases roughly in proportion to the amount of traffic available. The traffic has increased a great deal in the last few years and I believe it will continue to increase at an accelerated rate. Very soon it will reach the point where in my judgment the present system will be a more costly way of providing that service than will a causeway. When a causeway is built it is the initial capital cost, the capital charges for the money invested, that are the greatest expense; but once it is built it will be able to carry a volume of traffic much larger than that now offering, and there would be no increase in cost in proportion to the increase in traffic, at least for a very long time. I am interested in having as clear and precise a statement as the minister can make on this matter.
I have promised that.

I am aware that the minister has promised to make such a statement, but time is passing and the people of Prince Edward Island and no doubt of other areas are most anxious to know what the situation is. The minister may recall that when he sat on this side of the house, his colleague, the present Minister of Transport, was extremely anxious to see that progress was being made as rapidly as possible, and because the rate of progress was not as great as the present Minister of Transport thought it should be at that time he was everlastingly asking questions of the then minister of public works. I remember that on one occasion he got up and asked if the causeway was now under construction. I am aware of course that it is not even yet under construction. On one occasion he saw fit to rechristen it "the pauseway", not the causeway. In passing I point out that the last few months have been the longest period there has been without any very illuminating statement from the government as to what is taking place.
I do not want to be political in any way because this is a great construction project and a great national undertaking. It will be unique in North America, indeed in the world, having regard to all the difficulties that exist in this area such as the ice problem, the tidal problem and so on. The Chesapeake bay causeway is similar in many respects, but there are some ways in which the Northumberland strait crossing will present additional problems. In that regard I should like to be sure that the Department of Public


Works has taken action to make certain that all the knowledge gained from the construction of the Chesapeake bay causeway can be exploited by the designers and the department in considering the construction of the Prince Edward Island causeway.
There is a great deal of doubt in people's minds, of course, as to what form it will take. I believe I am correct in assuming that if it involves tunnels in part it would then be impractical or at least very costly to accommodate a railway line. This has grave implications. If that is so we would like to know what the thinking as to an alternative is. Would it be considered advisable to continue to use one ferry for rail service only for a period of time? It is most important at this stage that a study should be made with regard to whether it is economically feasible, and feasible in other ways, to contemplate having Prince Edward Island do without rail service entirely. I know of course, as everybody knows, that there is a trend toward the abandonment of railway lines; but whether or not it would be feasible to carry on a developing economy in the whole of Prince Edward Island with no rail service at all is something that should be studied. A conclusion should be reached one way or the other before consequent decisions are made. If it is decided that rail services are not necessary there is the question of alternate road construction to take the place of railway services. I do not want to prolong the discussion and I have nothing more to say at the moment.

Mr. Chairman, I was very pleased that the Minister of Public Works visited the west last summer. He did manage to get out there. In the house last year I suggested to him that he might visit southwestern Alberta and familiarize himself with the road situation there, with the idea that in his consideration of a second or alternate trans-Canada highway he might see his way clear to name the route from Lethbridge to Nelson as the best alternative to the national No. 1 trans-Canada highway.
I do not know what the minister did while he was out there. I had hoped he might get in touch with me so that I would be able to carry out the promises I made to him to take him around. However, he never showed up. I am afraid he only talked to certain people and did not see the right people. Nothing has happened with regard to this highway and we expected something more tangible. We would be only too glad to take

the minister fishing and extend to him all of the hospitality which the resources of that great region enable us to offer, but we also wish that he would familiarize himself with the problems of the area and talk to the people who know most about the problems there so that he would be in a position to act on them.
So far the people of Lethbridge and the Crowsnest pass area have heard nothing with regard to his views as to a southern highway. I see it is five o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and as I have not finished what I wanted to say I would ask to be allowed to call it five o'clock.
