On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I regret you were able to get on to this item, but a few years ago a practice was adopted of balloting for a place on this particular section of private members' business, so that hon. members were able to get a place at the head of the list with some prospect of having their bills debated.
During the last two years we have seen that this priority established through balloting seems to have become more or less meaningless. Many hon. members are interested in what appears in the order of balloting, but frankly one has to spend about half an hour or three quarters of an hour chasing around on Friday afternoons trying to find out what bill will be proceeded with. There are hon. members in the house interested in particular bills as they appear on the order paper and who are prepared to make contributions, but they cannot find out what bill will be dealt with until the very last.
There are hon. members interested in speaking on certain bills, but who actually leave on Friday mornings as they cannot find out whether tnose bills will be dealt with or not. At present there is a queue up from the beginning of the session, and I suggest there should be 24 hours notice of which bill is going to be debated at this time on Friday afternoons.
I suggest that this practice of standing bills has made a mockery of the balloting for priority and that we should not continue this practice. If there is going to be this wholesale standing of public bills, then there should be 24 hours notice given of what bill will actually be dealt with.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I wonder if I could speak to that point of order. When I was government house leader I instituted a procedure whereby when a private member's bill was called for the first time it was permitted, without any question, to stand. On the second oc-

Railway Act
casion it was called it was permitted to stand if there were a valid reason for so doing, if the hon. member were inexcusably absent or suffered from illness. On the third occasion it was called, then only if there was a very special reason for its retaining its position on the order paper was it so retained, but not otherwise. The result was that bills, having been called the second time and not proceeded with, dropped to the bottom of the order paper, and on a few occasions it was after they were called a third time that they were dropped to the bottom of the order paper.
Now you have bills standing on the order paper in the same position for the entire session. The result is that we never know what is coming up, and there should be some correction made to this procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If I may be allowed to speak to that point of order, it is quite true that there is likely to be some annoyance caused by the fact that bills might be stood for an indefinite period, but as we all know there are no definite rules covering the matter at the moment.
I am advised by the government whip's office that it has always been possible for a member inquiring from that office to ascertain in proper time, and well before the date, when a bill to be called will actually be discussed. There might be the odd exception, but I agree this would very probably be a good subject for discussion by the special committee of the house on procedure, and I should hope that one day we will reach a solution which will not only be empirical- like the one consisting of calling the whip's office, which is always at the disposal of hon. members-but a solution which will be written into the rules of the house.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with great respect to my hon. friend from Edmonton West I suggest that there is no point of order in the sense that any rule is being violated. The hon. member is making a suggestion as to a change that might be made, and I think there is merit to his suggestion, but I am sure Your Honour will agree that there is no point of order on the basis of which you can rule that we cannot proceed with the order now called.
We are acting under standing order 19 (1) and (2), a request having been made and concurred in by the government that certain bills might stand. All I am saying is that I think the point raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has validity,

but it is validity only as a suggestion, as something we should look at, not as something on which Your Honour can rule at this stage. I am sure my hon. friend will agree with me, and as a member of the special committee on organization and procedure I for one accept the suggestion that we should look into his proposal in that committee.

I would readily state that as a point of order I am not asking Your Honour to make a ruling on anything, but I am drawing something to the attention of the house, and that is the only way I could do it. I would point out to the house leader that the bills are stood at the request of the government, in conformity with the rules-
Yes, in conformity with the rules.

-because it is only the government which can ask to have them stand. As indicated by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), the government house leader has the remedy in his own hands. It is for the government to decide whether or not it will request to have a bill stood. It is for that reason I have raised the point of order this afternoon. I think Your Honour and other hon. members will recognize there are many other bills which have queued up behind the first 50 and which might have a chance to be debated if the ones in front were not stood en bloc. Some of these have now been stood 12 or 15 times.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am afraid that this point of order which, in fact, was a well taken suggestion and not a point of order, will soon become a question of privilege as far as I am concerned. I must add in due justice that there is also the empirical solution of the whips getting together and negotiating to convince the government not to stand a bill, if it is shown that there may be some prejudice. I repeat that on our part, and I think the feeling will be the same on all sides of the house, there is willingness that this suggestion should be transmitted to the committee on procedure for consideration. Indeed, it need not be transmitted formally because the learned chairman of that committee, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is here and will have heard the suggestion.

I am afraid I must question the propriety of the suggestion by the leader of the house that anyone wishing to find out what is likely to happen should get in touch with the government whips office. With all

due respect to the hon. gentleman there is a question as to the propriety of such a course of action and I think this should be taken into consideration.

I should like to ask the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) if he did contact his own whip's office in connection with the business before the house during the private members' hour today. We take the initiative. We may slip up sometimes, but we try to advise opposition whips of what is likely to be up for consideration. I have heard from my own office that the opposition whip's office was advised of today's business on Thursday at twelve noon.
As to the standing of some of these bills, as the hon. member knows, a rule of the house states that this must be done at the request of the government. We take this action in accordance with requests which come from other parties in the house; I think it is important, in my position, that we do retain some good will among ourselves concerning what goes on in the house.

In reply to the government whip may I say there have been many afternoons when at three o'clock the hon. gentleman or his assistant have been running around madly trying to determine what was going to happen. This may be a classic example of an occasion when the government whip can assume a mantle of virtue, but I suggest it is an exception.

May I point out in this connection that I inquired of my whip this afternoon what would be coming up during this particular hour and he informed me that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) would be dealing with one of his bills. I looked at the order paper with that understanding, and Bill No. C-9 was the first which came to my attention.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I can
understand the concern of the house over the procedure which has been followed since five o'clock today and on a number of other afternoons but I would say to hon. members that whatever procedure is adopted the Chair is guided by standing order No. 19. Possibly I could say to the hon. member for Edmonton West that I will take note of the suggestion he has made and as chairman of the committee bring it to the attention of Mr. Speaker.

If I may just say a word on the subject of procedure before we go on to consider the bill before us, let me point out that the whip's office asked me on Tuesday of this
Railway Act
week whether I was willing to proceed with this measure.
I am concerned about the amount of time which is being taken up during the so-called private members' hour for the consideration of this and similar matters. Last week discussion of the estimates cut into consideration of another bill in which I was interested for 12 minutes or so and now, I see, it is 18 minutes past five. As long as we continue with this so-called private members' hour I suggest it should really be 60 minutes and that in future, Mr. Speaker, you do not call it six o'clock until 60 minutes have expired. The committee on procedure might well come up with some change in our rules to make this possible. I would prefer the system they have in the United Kingdom where there are fewer bills but more time is allowed in which to discuss them. With those remarks I will move on to the subject of the bill before us.
This is an act to amend the Railway Act by requiring transportation companies operating under the Railway Act to file a copy of their reports with the House of Commons. My idea is that such reports should be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines where they could be examined. Officials of the companies in question could graph lines where they could be examined, by members of the committee as is done in the case of the Canadian National Railways.
I wish to comment on the work of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines in this connection. Prior to this session, the work of examining the annual report of the C.N.R. was done by a special sessional committee. This year we made it the work of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I think this was probably a sensible change. If hon. members will examine the most recent report of that committee they will become aware of some of the topics which were brought up by members. I will refer to a few of them now. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner) spent a considerable time questioning the management of C.N.R. about their policy in relation to rail line abandonment. He took, I thought, a great deal of time on this, but the subject was important to him, and no doubt to other members from the three prairie provinces, so I think the time was probably well spent.
The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) asked the president of the company questions about railway service to a steel complex which was contemplated in the province of Quebec. Both the hon. members

Railway Act
for Halifax brought up the question of rail traffic in that important port. The hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. Millar) asked the management of the company questions concerning their policy regarding employees who would be laid off as a result of the closing of railway shops at London, Ontario. The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) had questions to ask about run-throughs on the northern line of the C.N.R., on the effect of automation on employees and the impact upon the communities concerned as a result of changes in running schedules. A number of members asked questions about railway lines to various company plants.
These are important questions which affect the people in the ridings represented by the members I have named. I think this committee serves a very useful function. The work of the committee is uneven. Some members do not attend very well, others attend regularly. Some do not come well prepared; others do. They have read the reports and made themselves well informed on transportation matters. However, as I say, the committee serves a useful function because its members have a chance to meet face to face with the management of the railway company and ask questions directly. I think this is much more useful than putting questions on the order paper, speaking on the estimates of the Department of Transport of putting questions to the Minister of Transport (Mi*. Pickersgill) which may ultimately be answered after lengthy correspondence between the department and the railway company.
This is a direct way of putting questions and obtaining information. The president of the company is there; the comptroller is there, as is the secretary and other officials. They are ready to answer questions and the information comes forward quickly. I know the committee has been the object of a good deal of publicity in the past, but I maintain that a good rapport has been established between its members and the management of the company because of this direct personal contact.
I know the reason for Canadian National Railways coming before the committee; it is of course because it is owned by the government, and the government has to supply capital funds for the company and supply money to cover the operational losses. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I contend that the other railway companies in this country are not really private enterprises in the strict sense of the term. I said "other railway companies"; there
[Mr. Prittle.l
are quite a few in which hon. members may be interested. There is the Algoma Central, I believe it is called, in northern Ontario; the Northern Alberta, the Pacific Great Eastern, and some of the American lines which run into Canada. But I refer particularly to the Canadian Pacific Railway and I would not try to disguise the fact that I would like to see this railway company's officials appear before the committee.
The Canadian Pacific is a private enterprise in the sense that its shares are not held by the government. But it is very much a public institution. It was established as a result of public policy; public lands were granted to it, and it still receives public moneys. All the railways in this country receive a great deal of public money. There are the bridge subsidies, the maritime freight subsidies, the other freight subsidies, the proposed Crows-nest pass subsidy-which I believe we will be dealing with later-and the proposed passenger subsidy. All the subsidies amount to a very large sum of money. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I submit that public money is being spent here and the representatives of the public ought to have the opportunity to question the management of the railway companies. Some operating rule may have to be worked out. Perhaps we should question the officials of those railway companies receiving subsidies of $5 million a year or more; I am not sure. But again, the point is that public moneys are being spent, and these railways affect the communities in this country and the lives of its people.
I said a few minutes ago that I should like to see the Canadian Pacific Railway Company management appear before the railway committee of the house. It seems rather incongruous that we have Canadian National appearing before this committee, where all its operations are subject to question-its railway operations, its steamship operations, its hotel operations, its trucking operations, its express operations and its telecommunications operation. All these matters are subject to questioning by the representatives of the people. But the other large transportation complex of this country is free of such investigation. I think it would serve a useful purpose to have these other companies appear before the committee, so they could be questioned about their operations by the representatives of the people who in one way or another pay the costs of the operations.
There is one particular point about the Canadian Pacific operation which I think is interesting and which is beginning to develop

at the present time. As is the case with the C.N.R., the Canadian Pacific has, besides its railway lines, steamship lines, trucking lines and telegraph operations. It owns lands from which revenues are received from the production of oil and gas. In my own province it owns land from which revenues are received from the cutting of timber; and it has a great many non-rail operations. According to the financial reports that I have read, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has set up another firm, an associated firm, called Canadian Pacific Investments Limited, and they are gradually turning over to Canadian Pacific Investments Limited many of their non-rail holdings. I should like to read a sentence or two from the September, 1964 report of the investment company of McLeod, Young, Weir & Company. They have this to say in part:
As the result of the transfer of many non-rail assets to the recently created subsidiary, Canadian Pacific Investments Limited, C.P.R.'s real earnings are now considerably understated, since C.P. Investments earnings are not consolidated with those of the railway company.
I do not want to make too much of that, Mr. Speaker, because I really have not investigated it very thoroughly. I have read this report by McLeod, Young, Weir & Company and I have read reports in the Financial Post and Financial Times on the same subject. I am simply trying to point out that this is a very important topic in which the members of this house might be interested; because I think some of us would be concerned if the company was not showing, in its railway operations, its total revenues. After all, the revenues and profits

the earnings, in other words-of the railway company certainly have some bearing upon the freight and passenger rates which are set.
The company received public lands at one time-a very large acreage of public lands; over 25 million acres, anyway-in western Canada. It is from these lands that revenues are being received from oil and gas production and in the sale of real estate, in some cases. In the city of Vancouver they are realizing large amounts of money from the sale of real estate. They would not have received these lands had they not been a railway company; and I contend that all these earnings should be taken into account when we are assessing the earnings position of the railway company and the relation they have to the freight and passenger rate structure within the country.
From time to time in the past we have had set up royal commissions to investigate trans-
Railway Act
portation. It seems to me that if there could be an annual review of the operations of our major transportation companies, the members of the House of Commons could meet the management directly and ask questions. Then there would be less need for investigation, less need for boards of inquiry. The information would be readily forthcoming each year and, despite the newspaper headlines which have attended the meetings of the railway committee at times, I still maintain there is a very good rapport between the members of this house and the management of the railway. We meet Mr. Donald Gordon; we speak to him; we see the other members of his staff. We can meet these people every year, and I think this is an excellent thing. I believe it should also be done with the other railway companies. I do not think the railways should be unwilling to appear before the committee, because whenever a royal commission has been set up and they have wanted to present their case they have been quite eager to appear before them. I think it would be good for them, as well as for the House of Commons.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, because the major transportation companies-the major railway companies particularly-affect the economy of communities throughout this country and the lives of individuals, and because the Canadian people have put up so much money for their operation, I think it is only right and proper that the representatives of the Canadian people in this house should have an opportunity of questioning and examining the management of these companies each year, as is now done in the case of Canadian National Railways.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the speech just made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie).
I appreciate that the hon. member's remarks were in the interest of the people and were not made for any political consideration.
I understand he is only looking forward to the protection of all concerned, and I want to commend him for his good intentions. But, as it happens so often when one wants to do something too well, one loses sight of one's goal; that is, unfortunately, the case with this Bill No. C-55. I fear it is exactly what would happen should the house pass such a piece of legislation. As a matter of fact, in my opinion, this could cripple any

Railway Act
action on the part of those who are engaged in or who favour private enterprise.
By submitting them-more specifically the Canadian Pacific-to such legislation, they would be compelled as is the case for publicly-owned companies, to submit to government interference in the internal administration of their affairs.
Many would no longer care to serve the community well, even while expecting a fair retribution.
I am not against some form of control, especially when people are being exploited, with regard to the conditions under which they work, the hours they work or the salary they are paid, far from it. But today, labour unions are so well organized and efficient that abuses are seldom to be deplored.
The purpose of this bill, according to the explanatory notes, is to permit parliament to inquire into, as is done with the publicly-owned Canadian National Railways, the financial structure and the operations of those private railway, telegraph and express companies and water carriers which come under the board of transport commissioners as public utilities.
I share some of the views of the previous speaker but I should like perhaps not to dispute their validity, but to express my concern over a far reaching socialism, a provident state that paralyses or tends to annihilate personal efforts without people realizing it.
Besides, it is provided in the charter of railways or public utilities having to do with transportation, that annual reports must be submitted to the board of transport commissioners and also to the dominion bureau of statistics, and I fail to see the need for such government interference as provided for in this legislation. I realize that some companies are virtual monopolies, but the brain behind them belongs to an individual at the service of a private organization, most often his own. His talent is put at the service of those who benefit from his activities; he pays salaries and in many cases, his employees, at least the most qualified, get fringe benefits according to their qualifications or years of service. In many cases, they are considered as partners rather than employees and relations between employees and employer do not have the tendency that is too often observed among the employees of an organization that is public property.
I would not go so far as saying that the C.N.R. personnel, and especially the express employees do not carry out their duty. Far

from it; but I claim, Mr. Speaker, that the interest in one's job, in those public companies, is very often limited, strictly to the terms of the contract agreed to. In this age of automation, everybody must face realistically the facts of life. Like many others, I would look unfavourably upon government control of private enterprise which always remains the best incentive for individual effort, the best way to think and believe that if the government must help the individual, the latter on the other hand must not expect everything from the government.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I wanted to make a few remarks on behalf of private enterprise, which should not be destroyed, which should be allowed to live if we are to have good understanding and to get results in our world.
Such are the remarks I wished to make and I made them not in the interest of one company or of one organization but in the interest of every one of us, namely of the people of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few very brief comments on the bill before us this evening, Bill No. C-55 to amend the Railway Act. I have listened with interest to the remarks made by the mover of the bill, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie;. As 1 understand the bill, the explanatory notes and the explanation of the hon. member, its purpose is to enable parliament to look into the financial structure and operations of private companies doing business in the field of transportation, telephones and telegraphs. The bill would add an additional subsection (5) to the other four subsections of section 384 of the act. This proposed amendment would make these companies submit an additional copy of their returns to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), who in turn would have to lay such copy before the house within a certain period.
I must agree with the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Rochon) that the proposed amendment to the Railway Act is unjustified because the Railway Act already provides for the filing of annual returns. The annual reports of these private companies already have under the act to be filed with the board of transport commissioners as well as with the dominion bureau of statistics. We can see why the C.N.R., the Canada Council or other crown corporations such as Trans-Canada Air Lines, or I should say Air Canada, would have to make annual reports to parliament. They are

822S
crown corporations. But I fail to see why private companies should be investigated by parliament. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that by poking our parliamentary noses into private business we are transgressing, reaching beyond our duties and trespassing on a field which lies entirely outside our proper jurisdiction. If we start snooping into the books of private firms, where do we stop? Where do we draw the line between private companies and crown corporations; between free enterprise and socialism? It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment before us would simply tie another governmental string and another yard of red tape around the neck of the private business.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-55, which is an act to amend the Railway Act, would force all private railways, telegraph, telephone, express companies and carriers by water, which now come under the board of transport commissioners, to be investigated each year by the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. Little does the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie), who is the sponsor of this bill, realize that all these companies must appear before the board of transport commissioners each time they intend to change their tariffs. All the pros and cons in respect of such a change are investigated, studied, and subject to a judgment after all witnesses have presented their cases. If the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond is not satisfied with the operations of any of these privately owned companies, and can support his case, he has the right as a Canadian citizen to appear before the board of transport commissioners.
I am very strongly in favour of private enterprise. Since I have visited many countries of Europe, and particularly some of the socialistic countries, I am even more strongly in favour of private enterprise. Our high standards of living and our way of life is the result of a private enterprise system and not the result of any socialistic measures in Canada. I will always be against anything or anyone who wants to socialize private enterprise in Canada.
In fact, I even believe that the C.N.R. should not be government owned, but should be owned privately. I feel the government should only enter into business activity in Canada when private people are not able to provide efficient service. The Canadian Pacific Railway has done a wonderful job in Canada in providing transport throughout the country.
Railway Act
I do not believe the government has any place in the ownership of the Canadian National Railways, but that it should be put back into the hands of private enterprise so long as it can be run efficiently.
I think also that the government should relinquish its ownership of Trans-Canada Air Lines to private enterprise. We have other air lines operating in Canada, such as the Canadian Pacific Airlines, which is carrying out an efficient operation. I strongly believe that the government should get out of the ownership of transportation services and allow private enterprise to own these companies, as long as the services are continued on an efficient basis.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with considerable interest to the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat, and I agree with him that private enterprise, in initiating the system we have today, has built Canada for the most part into what it is today. I think this practice should be continued and encouraged because this is the most efficient way of developing a country.
I believe I should say that I do not agree with him in some of his arguments, for the very reasons he has advanced. If the C.P.R. was in effect running its operation as a free enterprise company and was not coming to parliament for subsidies I would support the kind of action which would keep what has been referred to as our parliamentary nose out of its business.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) presented a very good case in support of making the financial affairs of the Canadian Pacific Railway known to parliament, and I agree with many of his reasons. We are now paying to the Canadian Pacific Railway something like $70 million annually in unconditional subsidies. Surely the members of this House of Commons have a right to know why the C.P.R. requires this kind of assistance. A few days ago when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) was introducing a resolution respecting the new Bill C-120, he said that he hoped to reach the position where all subsidies paid directly to railway companies will be paid for specific purposes, and that massive unconditional subsidies will no longer exist.
Before the end of this session I think we shall have the opportunity of examining the officers of the Canadian Pacific Railway in respect of that company's financial affairs, because no doubt those officers will be pre-
822S

Railway Act
senting themselves to a parliamentary committee, along with their briefs and requests for assistance. However, following the meetings of that committee this session I feel, as the hon. member who supports this bill has advocated, that in view of the fact the C.P.R. does require government subsidy, parliament should have the right to examine its financial structure, its profit and loss statements and balance sheet, as it should have the right to examine the financial structure of any company which comes to parliament asking for millions of dollars in unspecified or unconditional grants. As long as these subsidies are being paid to the C.P.R., or to any other company, even though I am in favour of free enterprise I feel as a member of parliament I have a right to know that they do in fact require this assistance. How can I satisfy myself in that regard unless I have the opportunity to examine their statements and crossexamine the officers of the companies?
If the railway companies, and this includes the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. as well as air lines, as the hon. member has said, carry on operations efficiently and provide the services required by the Canadian people without requiring subsidies from the federal treasury, they should be able to operate without our sticking our parliamentary nose into their affairs. However as long as we are required to pay literally hundreds of millions of dollars out of the public treasury to assist these transportation systems, I feel we have a right to know what their financial structures are. I might say also-
Would we have time to examine it?
Yes, we would have time to examine it.
It would be a 12-month session.

I might say also that, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) pointed out, there were certain cash grants made out of the public treasury, along with public lands and so on in setting up the Canadian Pacific Railway in the first place. However, when they come back to parliament wanting to raise freight rates, for example, they only present a picture of their financial affairs which is specifically confined to the railway operations. There is the Canadian Pacific Oil and Gas Company, what I believe is referred to as the Canadian Pacific investment fund and so on. A large part of the assets that were turned over to Canadian
[Mr. Olson.l
Pacific when it was established in the first instance are vested in these separate companies. Whether you want to call it free enterprise, public enterprise or any other kind of enterprise, if justice is to be done all of these things, because they were a consideration in the first place, need to be taken into consideration before any further support for the railways from the public purse can be justified. Therefore I think it is a perfectly justifiable demand that the officers of these companies should be called before a committee of parliament so that we can examine the whole of their operations, rather than having to be content with just what they choose to give us.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) was certainly well intentioned in introducing his bill. Nevertheless, there are a few comments I should like to make, inasmuch as I am against its principle.
What the hon. member said about his bill in no way convinced me that it ought to be supported. Of course, in the case of the Canadian National Railways or Air Canada, which are crown corporations property of the Canadian people, it is perfectly logical and legitimate for members of this house to have the right to look into their financial operations. When those companies appear before a committee of this house, members can get information about their financial structure, their development and their programs. We recognize that there are cases where such a thing can clear things up. The Canadian people certainly wish to be informed about their activities through members of parliament.
If we recognize this principle in the case of crown corporations we cannot do so, however, so far as private companies mentioned in the bill are concerned. The hon. member referred especially to the C.P.R. in support of his bill, mentioning that this company had obtained public funds for its operations. He only referred to that company, but on the other hand, his bill goes much further. As a matter of fact, it mentions private railway, telegraph and transportation companies already coming under the board of transport commissioners. Now, those private companies are already required to submit returns to the board of transport commissioners which has jurisdiction over a great number of their activities. It would be quite another thing, as suggested by an hon. member, if those companies published each year a report

which, to all practical purposes, would be a public document because it would come before parliament. Thus all companies could find out the assets, liabilities and operating costs of all other companies, which would certainly be harmful to the latter's interests.
Private companies have to comply with a lot of regulations, they are obliged to submit statistics and reports to the federal and provincial governments, and I think that we must not go any further in that field. Companies already have to hire experts to prepare all the statistics and other information required by regulations and federal as well as provincial laws. They must not be forced to appear before the railway committee or the board of transport commissioners to answer publicly all sorts of questions on their operations.
Of course, nothing stops the committee from making certain suggestions when it considers the reports of crown corporations, but it can do so only up to a point. Private companies cannot be influenced substantially
Railway Act
as far as their operations are concerned nor can their reports be examined, because such a study must be carried out by experts of the board of transport commissioners. Those people are the only ones who can scrutinize the operations of the companies in question. At any rate, such an examination would be too heavy a task for the committee; the latter would have to sit all year round to make a detailed study of the balance sheets and operations of those companies.
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, this bill will be a handicap to private enterprise which has done so much for the country. Furthermore, it is not only premature, it serves no useful purpose.
May I call it six o'clock?
